articles.body:
Ministro Leonardo Barchini no programa Bom Dia, Ministro. — Foto: Reprodução.

Às vésperas do primeiro dia do Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) 2026, no qual alunos fazem a redação e respondem questões de linguagens e ciências humanas, o ministro da Educação, Leonardo Barchini, comentou sobre a expectativa em torno do tema da redação deste ano.

"Os temas das redações do Enem todo ano têm uma certa polêmica, mas são temas muito aderentes ao que estamos vivendo na época, ao nosso tempo, e é assim que tem que ser, porque o Enem é uma prova que testa os conhecimentos gerais e testa aquilo que o estudante está vivendo", disse Barchini no programa Bom Dia, Ministro, nesta quarta-feira (4).

O ministro também reforçou que não tem acesso antecipado ao tema da redação .

O Enem 2026 acontece nos dias 8 e 15 de novembro. Neste ano, mais de 5 milhões de participantes tiveram a inscrição confirmada e estão aptos a participar do exame.

articles.title: Alcolumbre quer votar nesta quarta PEC da redução da maioridade penal em busca de apoio da direita para reeleição | G1
articles.body:
Em um acordo fechado de última hora no plenário, após a aprovação da proposta de emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública , o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), acertou a tentativa de votação nesta quarta-feira (4) de uma PEC para reduzir a maioridade penal.

A ideia é que os senadores Camilo Santana (PT-CE), líder do PT, e Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) cheguem a um acordo em torno de um texto de consenso.

A iniciativa é um aceno de Alcolumbre à direita, onde busca votos para garantir sua recondução à presidência do Senado ( entenda mais abaixo ).

Nesta terça (3), os governistas conseguiram evitar que duas emendas que tratavam da redução da maioridade penal fossem votadas junto com a PEC da Segurança Pública.

Por um placar apertado, de 38 a 36, o plenário decidiu retirar o tema do texto e transformá-lo em propostas separadas.

O resultado mostrou que a direita não tinha, naquele momento, votos suficientes para aprovar uma PEC. Uma emenda constitucional precisa do apoio de pelo menos 49 dos 81 senadores, em dois turnos de votação.

Não interessa a Alcolumbre, porém, impor uma derrota definitiva à direita, onde busca apoio para garantir sua recondução à presidência do Senado . O acordo prevê acelerar a tramitação da PEC para tentar votá-la diretamente no plenário.

A tentativa de aproximação com a direita ocorre em meio à campanha de Alcolumbre para continuar na presidência do Senado a partir de 2027.

O senador tenta construir uma maioria que inclua parlamentares da oposição e tem como uma de suas principais estratégias dividir a bancada do PL.

O partido terá a maior bancada do Senado e discute lançar Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) contra Alcolumbre.

Nas últimas semanas, o presidente do Senado também vinha discutindo pautas de interesse da direita na tentativa de ampliar seu apoio nesse campo

Na saída do plenário, Alcolumbre confirmou ao blog que vai tentar votar nesta quarta a redução da maioridade penal.

À mesa, presidente do Senado Federal, senador Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), conduz sessão. — Foto: Carlos Moura/Agência Senado

As propostas em discussão têm diferenças. O texto defendido pelo PL reduz a maioridade penal para 16 anos em crimes de menor gravidade e para 14 anos em crimes hediondos.

Já a proposta de Camilo Santana reduz a maioridade para 16 anos apenas nos crimes hediondos, mantendo a regra atual para os demais delitos.

Durante o segundo turno da eleição presidencial, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) concordou, pela primeira vez, com a redução da maioridade penal para 16 anos nos casos de crimes hediondos.

A proposta foi defendida por Camilo Santana, que atuou como um dos coordenadores da campanha de Lula na etapa final da eleição.

articles.title: Douglas Ruas: Paes pede investigação por compra de votos no Rio | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato derrotado acusa chapa eleita de abuso de poder, desinformação eleitoral e compra de votos. Ação apresentada ao TRE-RJ também pede inelegibilidade por oito anos.
articles.summary: A ação de Eduardo Paes no TRE-RJ acusa Douglas Ruas de usar desinformação e compra de votos para vencer a eleição, pedindo a cassação e inelegibilidade do eleito.
articles.body:
A campanha de Eduardo Paes ( PSD ) acionou a Justiça Eleitoral para pedir a investigação de supostas irregularidades atribuídas a Douglas Ruas ( PL ) e à Coligação Rio Real nas eleições de 2026. Protocolada em 1º de novembro, a ação cita suspeitas de compra de votos e coação de eleitores, entre outras acusações, e pede a cassação do registro ou do diploma de Ruas.

O documento apresenta denúncias, registros policiais, reportagens e publicações em redes sociais como indícios para sustentar as alegações. As acusações ainda serão analisadas pela Justiça Eleitoral e não representam, por si só, comprovação das irregularidades.

Segundo a ação, há quatro eixos principais de suspeita: distribuição de propaganda considerada enganosa, circulação de santinhos apócrifos, registro de votos nulos com o número 13 e suposta compra ou coação de eleitores.

Segundo a petição, a campanha de Ruas contratou a produção de 100 mil panfletos intitulados "DOUGLAS RUAS - EVANGÉLICO", pagos com recursos do Fundo Especial de Financiamento de Campanha (FEFC).

O material atribuía a Eduardo Paes posições favoráveis ao aborto, à liberação de drogas e a banheiros unissex, entre outros temas. Os advogados de Paes afirmam que as informações eram falsas e buscavam influenciar o eleitorado religioso.

A ação também questiona o panfleto "RIO ESCOLHE", que associava Paes ao então candidato à Presidência Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva e destacava o número 13. Segundo a acusação, a propaganda poderia induzir eleitores a digitar 13 para governador, embora o número de Paes fosse 55.

A petição argumenta que 204.309 votos para governador foram anulados com o número 13 . Ruas venceu no primeiro turno com 4.271.199 votos, ou 50,88% dos válidos, contra 3.706.984 de Paes, ou 44,16%.

Os autores argumentam que, se esses votos tivessem sido destinados a Paes, Ruas teria ficado abaixo de 50% dos válidos e a eleição iria ao segundo turno. A relação entre os votos nulos e o material de campanha, no entanto, ainda precisa ser demonstrada no processo.

Santinhos e suspeitas de compra de votos

A ação também relata a circulação de santinhos que associavam a foto e o nome de Paes ao número 22, usado por Ruas. Segundo a petição, parte do material não apresentava identificação do contratante ou da gráfica.

Entre os episódios citados para sustentar as suspeitas de compra de votos está a apreensão, em Niterói, de R$ 600 mil em espécie e planilhas com Priscila Alencar dos Santos, filha da deputada federal Soraya Santos (PL). A petição pede que a origem e o destino do dinheiro sejam investigados. A apreensão, por si só, não comprova compra de votos.

Em Teresópolis, a ação cita ainda a apreensão de materiais de campanha de Ruas, um crachá de fiscal partidário e R$ 2 mil em dinheiro dentro de um veículo no dia da votação.

Também foram incluídas denúncias sobre suposta compra e coação de eleitores em diferentes regiões do estado. Publicações no X, Instagram, Threads, Facebook e Reddit relatam pagamentos de R$ 50 a R$ 200 em troca de votos.

Para aprofundar a investigação, os advogados pedem que as plataformas forneçam dados de mais de 60 perfis citados no processo, para que os responsáveis pelas publicações possam ser identificados e eventualmente ouvidos como testemunhas.

A ação também solicita o compartilhamento de procedimentos e investigações da Polícia Federal, Polícia Civil, Ministério Público Eleitoral e órgãos de fiscalização eleitoral relacionados aos episódios mencionados na petição.

articles.title: PEC da Segurança: janela de oportunidade para o governo e Alcolumbre | G1
articles.standfirst: Disputa em torno da proposta expôs as dificuldades de articulação do Planalto e deu ao presidente do Senado uma oportunidade de fortalecer seu projeto de reeleição.
articles.summary: A PEC da Segurança virou trunfo para a reeleição de Davi Alcolumbre no Senado, enquanto o governo Lula lida com a pressão pela redução da maioridade penal.
articles.body:
A discussão sobre segurança pública ganhou força após o primeiro turno, marcado pelo desempenho do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) à frente de Lula ( PT ) naquele momento, e pela formação de uma maioria conservadora no Congresso Nacional .

Diante desse cenário, a estratégia do governo e do candidato à reeleição foi intensificar o debate sobre segurança pública. A oposição, por sua vez, condicionou o apoio à PEC da Segurança Pública à inclusão da redução da maioridade penal, colocando o governo em uma situação delicada.

O presidente do Senado , Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), estava enfraquecido pelo resultado eleitoral em seu estado e pela composição do casa após as eleições. Precisava, portanto, oferecer apoio ao governo para conseguir ajuda em seu projeto de reeleição, prevista para fevereiro.

O movimento avançou quando Alcolumbre sinalizou que colocaria a proposta em votação. A oposição, então, aproveitou a oportunidade para pressionar o governo: afirmou que seria favorável à PEC, mas condicionou o apoio à inclusão da redução da maioridade penal.

A questão era delicada para o governo, que não tinha articulação suficiente para garantir o apoio de sua base mais à esquerda e progressista à redução da maioridade penal. O tema ganhou destaque na entrevista de Lula ao Jornal Nacional , quando o presidente declarou, pela primeira vez, s er favorável à redução da idade penal para 16 anos.

Sem articulação para aprovar a matéria e sem condições de entrar em uma votação com risco de derrota, o governo ficou em uma posição difícil. Alcolumbre, então, atuou pela segunda vez e retirou a proposta da redução da maioridade penal de pauta.

Agora, o assunto volta ao debate por causa de uma janela de oportunidade na próxima legislatura. O ano está chegando ao fim, e o Congresso precisa votar o orçamento. Além disso, a nova composição do Legislativo, com um perfil ainda mais conservador, pode dificultar a aprovação da proposta nos moldes pretendidos pelo governo.

articles.title: Operação Agulhas Negras reúne 2 mil militares no Vale do Paraíba | G1
articles.standfirst: Atividades seguem até domingo (8) com uso de blindados, aeronaves e balsas em simulações de defesa e transposição de rio.
articles.summary: Treinamento mobiliza tropas e blindados em oito cidades para testar a prontidão do Exército Brasileiro em combates e na transposição de rios.
articles.body:
Cerca de 2 mil militares do Exército Brasileiro participam, ao longo desta semana, de um treinamento operacional em oito cidades do Vale do Paraíba e em Resende , no sul do estado do Rio de Janeiro. Batizada de Exercício Agulhas Negras 2026, a mobilização segue até domingo (8) e reúne tropas de mais de 20 unidades militares sediadas no estado de São Paulo.

O treinamento anual simula cenários de combate por terra, água e ar para testar a capacidade de reação das Forças Armadas. Na missão proposta neste ano, os militares precisam avançar pelo território regional para reconquistar uma área fictícia invadida por forças inimigas em Resende.

As ações ocorrem em áreas estratégicas dos seguintes municípios:

Militares reunidos para o Exercício Agulhas Negras — Foto: Divulgação/Comando da Aviação do Exército

Por conta da operação, o Exército informa que moradores e motoristas podem encontrar comboios de viaturas caracterizadas, veículos blindados e militares fardados em deslocamento pelas cidades e pela Rodovia Presidente Dutra (BR-116) até o fim de semana.

Veja como funciona a travessia no Rio Paraíba do Sul

Uma das etapas práticas do exercício aconteceu na manhã desta quarta-feira (4), às margens do Rio Paraíba do Sul, no bairro Vila Portugal, em Lorena. No local, equipes de engenharia prepararam as margens do rio e montaram estruturas flutuantes para fazer a transposição das tropas e de veículos pesados.

Com o auxílio de barcos de manobra e de uma balsa militar, o efetivo treinou a travessia de blindados e caminhões que pesam cerca de 20 toneladas. Segundo o Exército, a atividade avalia a rapidez e a precisão das equipes tanto para situações de conflito armado quanto para missões de ajuda humanitária, quando pontes ou estradas ficam interditadas.

Militares durante treinamento no Rio Paraíba do Sul — Foto: Reprodução/TV Vanguarda

Em Taubaté, o treinamento também movimentou a base do Comando da Aviação do Exército (CavEx), no bairro Itaim, de onde partiram helicópteros usados no transporte de tropas e no apoio aéreo às ações em solo.

A mobilização na região reproduz uma operação ofensiva de guerra para testar como mais de 20 batalhões paulistas funcionam juntos no mesmo terreno. Durante a semana, infantes, pilotos, engenheiros e operadores de blindados precisam sincronizar a comunicação e o avanço das tropas sob pressão, simulando a defesa das fronteiras e do território nacional contra uma invasão estrangeira.

Segundo o comandante da Brigada de Infantaria Aeromóvel, general Aires, o foco do treinamento é exercitar na prática o papel constitucional da força terrestre na proteção do país.

"Esse é um exercício, basicamente, num contexto de defesa externa. É a nossa missão precípua constitucional, é a garantia da soberania do país", explica o general.

Para o comandante do 28º Batalhão de Infantaria Mecanizado, coronel Fernando Griep de Souza Franco, tirar o efetivo dos quartéis para atuar em conjunto no campo eleva o preparo técnico dos militares. "É bastante desafiador, mas muito gratificante. A gente tem um ganho profissional enorme, contribui imensamente para a coesão e para o engrandecimento do espírito de corpo da tropa", afirma.

O exercício em larga escala também coloca jovens recém-incorporados em funções reais de liderança e tomada de decisão em campo. É o caso do soldado Arthur Cordeiro, de 19 anos, que entrou para o Exército neste ano e já coordena uma equipe do 28º Batalhão de Infantaria Mecanizado como cabo de esquadra durante as missões.

"É uma experiência muito única, ainda mais no meu primeiro ano de Exército. É um privilégio estar podendo participar de um evento tão grande assim."

articles.title: Troy Jackson defeats longtime Maine Sen. Susan Collins
articles.summary: Democrat Troy Jackson defeated longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins in the Maine Senate race, CBS News projects.
articles.body:
Washington — Democrat Troy Jackson defeated GOP Sen. Susan Collins in the Maine Senate race , CBS News projects, in a key victory for Democrats who have sought for decades to oust the Republican senator.

Maine Democrats selected Jackson, 58, as their nominee in July, after the party's initial nominee Graham Platner withdrew following an allegation of sexual assault. Jackson, a fifth-generation logger who lost his bid for governor earlier this year, previously served as president of the Maine state Senate and has billed himself as a champion of the working class.

Jackson faced off against Collins, who was the sole Republican incumbent seeking reelection in a state Kamala Harris won in 2024, making the race Democrats' clearest pickup opportunity. But the five-term senator, with a history of breaking with President Trump, had survived political headwinds in the past. And after Democrats' chaotic primary process, Jackson's path to victory in the Pine Tree State remained tenuous.

Collins, 73, questioned Jackson's effectiveness as a legislator, while she touted the influence in the Senate that she has wielded for Maine's benefit. But Jackson argued Collins hasn't gone far enough in her opposition to the president, and zeroed in on her support for Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, which paved the way for the high court to overturn the federal right to an abortion in 2022.

The projected victory came after Democrats saw a series of flips in races that weren't initially expected to be competitive this cycle, after the unpopular war in Iran and persistently high gas and diesel prices expanded a map once favorable to the GOP.

articles.title: Republicans suffer historic Senate upset as Dem flips deep-red state for first time in nearly a century
articles.summary: Adam Hamilton ended nearly a century of Republican Senate dominance in Kansas by defeating Roger Marshall in a brutal midterm battle.
articles.body: The GOP's nightmare scenario became a reality in Kansas on Election Night, where an insurgent Democratic newcomer toppled a Republican incumbent for the first time in nearly a century. Megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton is projected to defeat first-term Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in one of the more unexpectedly close and brutal races during this midterm election cycle, according to the Fox News Decision Desk. Hamilton’s win in the Sunflower State marks the first time Kansans have sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.Marshall’s campaign sputtered in the late stages of the race, giving Hamilton an opening to peel off a large number of independent and rural voters — and it also dealt a bruising blow to Senate Republicans who are trying to cling to their slim majority in the upper chamber. MAINE, KANSAS SENATE RACES NECK AND NECK AS DEMOCRATS LEAD IN TEXAS, MICHIGAN, POLL SHOWS Democratic strategist Mally Smith told Fox News Digital that Adam Hamilton was the perfect candidate to run in Kansas. "He was able to bring Republicans, Independents and Democrats together to pull a stunning upset. The combination of a blue environment, a scandal-plagued incumbent, and a strong Democrat like Hamilton made this upset possible," said Smith. Though for months their race was not on the radar of national Democrats or Republicans, in the waning weeks, Marshall acknowledged that he was running for his political life as headwinds battered Republican incumbents across the country. "I think that, you know, I'm not a political expert, I'm a physician, but if we lose Kansas, I don't see how we keep control of the Senate," Marshall told Fox News Digital in an interview before the election. "And that's why a vote for Adam Hamilton is a vote for Chuck Schumer and Democrat control of the Senate," he continued. "It’s that simple." DEM SENATE HOPEFUL REJECTS SCHUMER BUT BENEFITS FROM MILLIONS IN SPENDING BY HIS ALLIES But Hamilton has time and again said that he would not support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to continue leading Democrats if elected, a point he reminded Marshall of during their final debate. "I’ve already said I wouldn't support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader if the Democrats took control of the Senate," Hamilton said. Their contest morphed into a bitter, bloody battle that dragged in millions of dollars in resources and high-profile surrogates, like President Donald Trump, who rallied there twice weeks and days before the election. TRUMP-BACKED SENATOR ADMITS GOP FACES NIGHTMARE SCENARIO IN STATE REPUBLICANS HAVEN'T LOST IN 90 YEARS It became dominated by brutal headlines against Marshall for his old medical practice, reportedly suing patients for unpaid bills, and searing ads against Hamilton that alleged he covered up sexual assault scandals at his church. Kansas political experts argued that the race was ripe for Hamilton to take, given that he had a built-in popularity within the state fostered by his decades as the head pastor and founder of the largest United Methodist church in Kansas and the political headwinds created by Trump’s policies — Marshall for much of the campaign remained closely aligned with the president. articles.title: LIZ PEEK: There may be a silver lining in Trump's brutal midterm defeat
articles.summary: Trump's midterm losses mirror Obama's 2010 rebuke, but Democrats now face governing without a clear plan to deliver on their affordability pledge. There could be a silver lining here.
articles.body: Midterm voters gave President Trump a "shellacking" on Tuesday, akin to that delivered to Democrat Barack Obama in 2010, when Republicans picked up 63 seats in the House and seven seats in the Senate. Though yesterday’s numbers were tempered by recent gerrymandering, the election was brutal for the GOP and for President Trump. Democrats gained control of both the House and the Senate on Tuesday. The numbers are not all in, but Democrats flipped at least seven Senate seats and more than a dozen House seats. The results in deep red Texas, where James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democratic senator from the Lone Star State in 33 years, were shocking but not entirely unexpected. Paxton was an unpopular candidate who carried a lot of baggage. That Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, putting a Democrat in the governor’s mansion for the first time in 32 years, was more stunning. TRUMP CONGRATULATES DEMOCRATS AFTER DOMINANT MIDTERMS, SAYS HE LOOKS FORWARD TO WORKING WITH THEM Equally stunning was that Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, the controversial anti-Israel progressive running for an open Senate seat in Michigan, beat former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers. One of the few bright spots for Republicans was Florida, where Republican Ashley Moody held her Senate seat, and Rep. Byron Donalds became the first Black governor of the state. As they did in 2010, Americans across the nation strongly rebuked the sitting president, declaring themselves unhappy with the first two years of his second term. Unfortunately for Republicans, questionable polling from many sources and President Trump’s low approval ratings turned out to be reasonably accurate predictors of the midterms. CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES My view is this: as in 2010, voters in this midterm cycle pummeled the incumbent for overreaching. Trump mistook his landslide 2024 win for a mandate, as did Obama. Both presidents offended voters by going too far — in Obama’s case, by trying to deliver on his campaign pledge to "change" the country. He forced through an unpopular massive healthcare program, turned our energy industries upside down by executive order, an effort later rejected by the courts, and ratcheted up government spending, which ushered in the Republican-led Tea Party. In President Trump’s case, he quickly closed the border, which voters demanded after his predecessor, Joe Biden, recklessly allowed millions of people to enter the country illegally. But he then pursued an aggressive effort to deport all undocumented people, including those who had lived in the U.S. for years and had committed no crime other than their original illegal entry. Voters did not approve of the resulting ICE-led confrontations, which in a couple of cases led to violent outcomes. Americans, who just months earlier had demanded secure borders, soured on the president’s signature immigration policies. DOUG SCHOEN: THE BIGGEST WINNER AND THE BIGGEST LOSER IN THE 2026 MIDTERMS Trump’s decision to wage war against Iran, in an effort to rid that state sponsor of terror of nuclear weapons, contradicted his campaign pledge to keep us out of foreign conflicts. Even those who supported Trump’s goal of preventing the mullahs from acquiring the deadliest of weapons lost patience as oil prices moved higher. Trump also unilaterally imposed tariffs on our trading partners, as he did in his first term, in order to level the playing field for U.S. companies. Though the White House can point to a rise in investment flowing into the U.S. and an upturn in domestic manufacturing as rewards for those measures, the president wielded his tariff weapon recklessly. DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR War-related jumps in gasoline and diesel prices combined with some inflation caused by Trump’s tariffs gave Democrats the opportunity to promise they would, if elected, deliver "affordability." It was an audacious claim, given that Joe Biden clobbered the country with a 21% jump in the cost of living during his four years in office, far surpassing what has happened under Trump. Nonetheless, Trump was punished for promising to bring prices down and failing to do so. Democrats running in the midterms had no real, specific agenda. Though they promise to deliver "affordability," they have not laid out how they will manage that. Some candidates have promised to implement Medicare for All to bring healthcare costs down, but fail to explain how they will come up with the estimated $25 to $50 trillion price tag. Some Democrats have run on reverting to Biden’s war on fossil fuels, but that will drive energy costs higher, not lower. TRUMP'S GAMBLE ON KEN PAXTON BACKFIRES AS DEMOCRAT PULLS OFF HISTORIC TEXAS SENATE UPSET Rather than laying out a specific platform, Democrats campaigned mainly on hating Donald Trump. He played into their hands by telling Americans to vote as if he were on the ballot. He was trying to drive turnout among his base, knowing that the left had fired up the opposition. But too many voters took him literally and voted against his party and him. The president will have to take responsibility for Republican losses. His policies were on the line, and in Texas and South Carolina he pushed forward flawed candidates. DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN Democrats will cheer their wins, but tomorrow, they will have to bring their fractured party together to govern. The progressive wing of the Democratic Party will push policies like Medicare for All, abolishing ICE and eliminating U.S. support for Israel, which the majority of Americans may not support. They will advocate for higher taxes and bigger welfare programs, risking U.S. credit ratings and driving up interest rates and inflation. Worse, some are calling to shut down the buildout of AI, risking U.S. dominance in the most important new technology of our time, as well as jobs, investment and economic growth. Oil and gas investment, too, is under threat from Democrats. Stock futures plunged overnight as Wall Street assessed what the election might mean. Two years of ugly conflict and internal divisions will not serve their party well and could jeopardize their presidential ambitions heading into 2028. If there is a silver lining in this harsh outcome for the GOP, it may be that Democratic dysfunction will undermine the momentum we saw Tuesday, allowing Republicans and President Trump to regroup. articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed delivers major blow to GOP in Michigan after bruising Senate race
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed toppled Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim U.S. senator, overcoming Trump's attacks on his faith and alleged foreign ties.
articles.body: Michigan is staying blue as Republicans’ hopes of flipping the state and gaining some breathing room in their thin majority were crushed. Abdul El-Sayed, who became the veritable face of this midterm cycle acting as the GOP’s boogeyman for Democratic policies across the country, is projected to topple former Rep. Mike Rogers in what was one of the most-watched contests of the election. In his victory speech, El-Sayed thanked AIPAC, which spent roughly $42 million running a campaign against him, for allowing him the opportunity to beat the American-Israeli interest PAC twice. El-Sayed celebrated his victory by invoking the Arabic phrase "alhamdulillah," which means "praise be to God." The progressive candidate also issued a warning shot to his defeated opponent, Rogers. "Enjoy your retirement," El-Sayed said of the Republican candidate. "You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again." Meanwhile, around 1 a.m. on Wednesday morning, Rogers called on his supporters to go home, sharing that it was going to be a "long night." Organizers shared with the Detroit News that the hotel needed them out by that time. ROGERS WARNS MICHIGAN VOTERS AGAINST EL-SAYED’S ‘EXTREME’ AGENDA AHEAD OF ELECTION Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed outran alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, concerns about his rhetoric over Israel and Jewish voters in Michigan and criticism from fellow Democrats for his ties to controversial political streamer Hasan Piker. Rogers failed to outrun the political headwinds that have buffeted Republicans this cycle, including affordability issues, President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada launched in the thick of the midterms and the Iran war, despite his attempts to distance himself and the administration from the latter issues. El-Sayed’s victory serves as a major blow to the GOP’s push against the progressive lean in Democratic politics, where for much of the cycle after his shock win over Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., Republicans painted him as the face of socialism and communism in their messaging. He will also be the first Muslim U.S. senator in history. His faith has been used as a line of attack by Republicans, including President Donald Trump, who last month during a rally in Michigan accused El-Sayed of being a "jihadist" that would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE "If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas," Trump said. Rogers similarly dipped into the same style of rhetoric, arguing to a crowd in Bad Axe, Mich., just days before the election that "This is not someone we can let into the United States Senate." "If you don't know Iran is our enemy, and you can't condemn a Hezbollah-inspired attack, you have no business being in the United States Senate," Rogers said. While Rogers and Republicans have run a national campaign against El-Sayed, the insurgent progressive has taken his own jabs at Trump, but largely ran a campaign focused on affordability issues in Michigan. EL-SAYED, ROGERS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD, TRUMP AND GUNS: 5 FIERY DEBATE MOMENTS "They want to point to me and my name and my faith as if somehow that’s the problem, but none of those things are what’s raising your gas prices or making a new home unaffordable," El-Sayed told reporters last month. The race attracted big names in both parties to stump for their respective candidates, with Trump, Vice President JD Vance, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and others making the pilgrimage to Michigan for Rogers. And Democratic heavyweights like former President Barack Obama, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., did the same for El-Sayed. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But El-Sayed’s win does not mean he will jump on board with the Democratic old guard in Washington, D.C. Like other progressives running for the Senate, he’s been publicly critical of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and would prefer Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., to lead Democrats in the Senate.

articles.title: 'Pod Save America' hosts call Democratic Party's midterm wins 'the end of the Trump era'
articles.summary: "Pod Save America" hosts celebrated Democratic midterm wins on "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" Tuesday night as the party was projected to retake control of Congress.
articles.body: The "Pod Save America" podcast team celebrated the Democratic Party's congressional wins in the midterm elections, calling the results "the beginning of the end of the Trump era" on "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" Tuesday night. "Pod Save America" hosts Jon Favreau, Jon Lovett, Dan Pfeiffer and Tommy Vietor appeared on the ABC late-night show as news outlets, including Fox News, projected that Democrats would win control of both chambers of Congress following the midterm elections. Kimmel asked whether they believed anyone from President Donald Trump's administration would be fired following the midterm election results. Vietor said he was unsure but expressed optimism about the country's direction. "I think that tonight is the beginning of the end of the Trump era in America," he said. CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES Kimmel noted earlier in the segment that all four men had worked in former President Barack Obama's administration during the 2010 midterm elections, when Democrats suffered major losses that Obama described as a "shellacking." Pfeiffer described the 2010 election as "one of the worst nights of our lives" but said he would enjoy seeing Trump administration staffers experience a similar feeling. "That night we went in, we knew it wasn't going to be great, so we had three scenarios: not that bad, kind of bad, pretty bad," Pfeiffer said. "We ended up with way worse than all of those. We were walking out of the White House at 3:00 in the morning. Rahm Emanuel, the chief of staff at the time, looked at us and said, 'Tomorrow is about to be the worst day of your life and everybody is going to call for you to be fired.' And he was right. It was terrible." "And I am going to enjoy every second of every Trump staffer feeling that way tomorrow," he added. DOUG SCHOEN: THE BIGGEST WINNER AND THE BIGGEST LOSER IN THE 2026 MIDTERMS Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment but did not immediately receive a response. During Fox News' live election-night coverage, Trump told "Special Report" anchor Bret Baier that he would use his presidential veto power if Democrats sent him legislation he opposed. "It's one of the stronger powers that a president has," Trump told Baier. "And they'll send over things that are insane and I'll veto them. And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll go out, and they'll say, how do we get this stuff done? And we'll work together." ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "You know, I have a lot of friends that are Democrats, believe it or not, I've already spoken to some of them. I've had four calls from meaningful Democrats and, people, in two senators and three congressmen, actually. So it's a total of five, and they have three waiting to call me. So I don't know, they obviously want to talk, but I have the power of veto. And the power of veto is, you know, it's impervious," he added.

articles.title: Dems flips yet another Senate seat in Trump country amid sweeping GOP upsets
articles.summary: Josh Turek's Iowa Senate win over Ashley Hinson marks the first time Democrats captured the seat since 2008 in a state Trump won by double digits.
articles.body: The Fox News Decision Desk projects that Democrat Josh Turek will win Iowa's open U.S. Senate seat, flipping a Republican-held seat as the GOP fights to retain control of the chamber. Turek defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson in the race to succeed retiring Sen. Joni Ernst. "Iowa, after 448 days of hard work, pushing up hills, knocking doors, visiting all 99 counties, visiting small and midsized communities all across Iowa, and preaching a message of a better future for Iowa – together, we have made history," Turek wrote on X. The victory marks the first time Democrats have won the seat since 2008, when former Sen. Tom Harkin secured his final term. It also represents a Democratic pickup in a state President Donald Trump carried by more than 13 points in 2024. SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY Senate Majority Leader John Thune had made Hinson’s race a priority, saying: "I’m absolutely convinced that she flat has to win, and if she doesn’t, we’re not going to be in the majority." Hinson shared with a crowd of supporters that she had conceded her race to Turek and congratulated him on a "very hard-fought campaign." "Josh and I, to put it mildly, disagree on a lot. But tonight I hope that we can agree on this, that the campaign is behind us, and the work of serving the people of Iowa remains ahead," Hinson said. "It is time to put politics aside, dial down the rhetoric, and start solving problems for Iowa's families and Iowa's farmers." Hinson then goes on to state that veterans, young people, students and millions of Americans need the help of politicians. "That's who this campaign was really for. And while tonight's outcome was not the one that we wanted, I am so deeply proud of our campaign's fight, and I am just eternally grateful to everyone who helped make that happen to all of you," Hinson said. Turek centered his campaign on affordability, healthcare and wages. He promised to push for lower prescription drug costs, more affordable housing, a higher minimum wage and a federal ban on food price gouging. DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE Healthcare was a personal theme for Turek, who was born with spina bifida and became a two-time Paralympic gold medalist. He pointed to his own experience accessing care and said, "healthcare is a human right." His platform also called for restoring Medicaid funding, protecting Affordable Care Act subsidies and supporting rural hospitals. Turek presented himself as a bipartisan lawmaker who could work across party lines, including on immigration. He campaigned as a "prairie populist," arguing that working families were being squeezed by housing, grocery and fuel costs while Washington politicians and corporations benefited. He also tied Iowa’s economic pressure to Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran. TRUMP-BACKED IOWA US SENATE HOPEFUL SAYS IRAN WAR MUST 'BE BROUGHT TO A SUCCESSFUL AND IMMEDIATE END' Hinson ran on tax relief, border security, parental involvement in schools and support for agriculture and biofuels. Trump backed her at a Sioux City rally, calling her "a mother, a warrior, a patriot" and promising that "with Ashley in the Senate, we will make it year-round E15. We’ll make it permanent." articles.title: Speaker Mike Johnson projected to cruise to re-election for fifth House term
articles.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson is seeking a fifth term representing Louisiana's 4th Congressional District in the House of Representatives.
articles.body: House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is poised to handily defeat his field of opponents to win a fifth term in the House of Representatives. Johnson, who enjoys a close relationship with President Donald Trump, is projected to win nearly 60% of the vote against four other declared candidates, according to The Associated Press, and therefore is guaranteed to return to Congress in January. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry modified this year's House elections after postponing the primaries to give the state legislature more time to redraw its congressional map to give Republicans an edge. BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES Instead of following the traditional schedule of a springtime primary race and a Nov. 3 general election, the top two candidates in each of the state's six House districts would advance to an early December runoff, unless one person clinches over 50% of the total vote. Louisiana's GOP majority scored a victory with the Supreme Court earlier this year that allowed it to essentially dissolve the state's one Black-majority district, which was drawn under guidelines set by the Voting Rights Act. THOMAS LEAVES NOTHING LEFT UNSAID ON RACIAL GERRYMANDERING DECISION: ‘GO FURTHER’ Johnson was widely expected to sail to victory on Tuesday night, given his leadership status and prolific fundraising. His seat in Louisiana's 4th Congressional District is anchored by Shreveport and Bossier City in the northwestern part of the state. Its rating with the nonpartisan Cook Political Report is R-26, making it a safe Republican territory. JOHNSON DELIVERS BIG FOR TRUMP, BUT FRUSTRATION GROWS ACROSS RAZOR-THIN GOP MAJORITY But his dominant performance on Tuesday night will not necessarily translate to further success within the House GOP conference. If Republicans keep their majority nationwide, Johnson is all but assured of remaining Speaker of the House in the next Congress. If they lose, Johnson is all but assured to face pressure from fellow House Republicans to step aside from his leadership role. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In the latter case, it's widely believed that House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, will face House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., for the minority leader position.

articles.title: GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts fends off independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska Senate race
articles.summary: NBC News projects Ricketts has won re-election after facing a competitive race in the traditionally red state.
articles.body: GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts has defeated independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, NBC News projects. Osborn, a pipe fitter, was one of multiple independent Senate candidates running this year in traditionally Republican states. Osborn had the added advantage of a one-on-one race against Ricketts after the Democratic nominee ended her campaign in July. But Osborn faced an onslaught of attacks accusing him of being a secret Democrat. He had stressed that he would not caucus with either party if he were elected, but he did have the backing of the Nebraska Democratic Party. Follow live updates on the midterm elections “Democrat Dan is too extreme, and he would be the most extreme senator we’ve ever sent to the U.S. Senate from Nebraska,” Ricketts said at a September debate. “And if he were in charge of the Senate and gave it to the Democrats, that would be a disaster for Nebraska.” The sharp attacks underscored the tougher-than-expected nature of the race in a state Donald Trump won by 20 points in 2024. The same year, Ricketts won a special election to serve the final two years of GOP former Sen. Ben Sasse’s term by 25 percentage points. Osborn, however, lost by just 7 points in his first Senate bid, against Republican Sen. Deb Fischer two years ago. Ricketts’ bid for a full Senate term became competitive amid Trump’s sinking approval ratings, with voters frustrated by high costs and the war with Iran. High diesel prices due to the war with Iran and Trump’s sweeping tariffs also hit farmers in heartland states, including Nebraska. At a rally in Nebraska in early October, Trump signed an executive order expanding access to diesel used in farming, known as “red dye” diesel. “Prices are all going down. Prices are all going way down, but they really are going to plummet as soon as that war ends. It’s going to be very soon,” Trump said at the rally. “And today, I’m announcing another unprecedented step to bring down costs for many years. Farm vehicles, construction equipment and other off-road vehicles have used what is known as ‘red dye’ diesel,” Trump said. “Do you know what that is? I don’t know what the hell it is, but whatever it is, it’s supposed to be very good.” Osborn, a Navy veteran and former union organizer, supported Trump’s move but described it as a “Band-Aid.” He often highlighted Nebraskans’ struggles with high costs, though he rarely directly criticized Trump by name in a state with plenty of his supporters. “I’ve gone around the state, and I’ve talked to thousands of Nebraskans and hardworking people — teachers, truck drivers, nurses, lunch ladies, you name it,” Osborn said at the debate. “I’ve talked to them, and people are working hard. But there’s a common theme that I find around the state, and times are getting harder. Costs are getting too expensive. Healthcare is getting too expensive. Groceries are too expensive, and families are falling behind.” Osborn also leaned into voters’ concerns about corruption, attacking Ricketts’ wealth and accusing him of being beholden to big donors and corporations. “People like us are tired of people in rooms like this calling the shots,” Osborn said in a TV ad featuring men gathered in a smoke-filled room. “But Pocket Pete, he’s right at home.” Ricketts also worked to remind voters that they elected him to statewide office in three separate elections, launching an ad focused on his time as governor. “Through fires and flooding, the ups and downs in agriculture, a global pandemic and every other challenge, Pete Ricketts has been there for Nebraska,” voters said in the ad.

articles.title: Midterms 2026: How Democrats built a blue wave and won control of Congress
articles.summary: Trump wasn't on the ballot. But exit polls suggested he was top of mind for voters.
articles.body:
It was a blue wave big enough to become a blue tsunami.

On Tuesday, the Democratic Party shattered a series of decades-long Republican winning streaks, notched several historic firsts and flipped both the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives as Americans in states and districts that voted to reelect President Trump just two years ago delivered a harsh judgment on the steep tariffs, rising gas prices, aggressive immigration raids and unresolved war in Iran that have so far dominated his second term.

"We didn't win this race by alienating our neighbors or shaming our neighbors or ridiculing our neighbors," Democrat James Talarico said after winning the Senate election in Texas. "We embodied a new kind of politics. A politics rooted in a deep love for our state, for our country and, most importantly, for all of our neighbors."

Votes were still being tallied and key races remained uncalled as Election Day came to an end. But as of 1 a.m. ET on Wednesday, when the last polls closed in Alaska, Democrats were projected to gain more than three dozen seats in the House and as many as nine seats in the Senate — far beyond the three and four seats, respectively, that they needed to retake each chamber. They were also on track to win the majority of governorships for the first time since 2011.

The list of milestones was long: The first Texas Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate since 1988 (Talarico). The first Latina ever elected governor of the Lone Star State (Gina Hinojosa). Kansas's first Democratic senator since the Great Depression (Adam Hamilton). The first Black woman governor in U.S. history (Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms). The first Democratic senator from South Carolina in decades (Annie Andrews). America's first Muslim senator (Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan). And what could be the largest Democratic House majority since 2008.

As a result, Trump will no longer enjoy complete Republican control of Congress. Starting in January, Democrats in the House and Senate will have the power to block parts of the president's agenda, reject his nominees, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again) .

Historically, midterms tend to be backlash elections; a president's party almost always sheds House seats when voters return to the polls to rate his first two years in office. The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six .

Yet some midterms are more momentous than others. In 2006, President George W. Bush's second midterm, Republicans lost 31 seats. In 2010, President Barack Obama's first midterm, Democrats lost 64 seats. And in 2018, Trump's first midterm, Republicans lost 42 seats.

This year, according to data journalist G. Elliott Morris , "Democrats have won the largest House popular vote victory for any party since 1974, when the Watergate scandal rocked Republicans to their core."

Here are four takeaways that help explain what happened in the 2026 midterms, and why.

The most striking thing about this year's Democratic gains is that they came in some of the redder parts of the country.

Before Election Day, the GOP's majorities on Capitol Hill were already narrow — a dynamic that usually limits the opposing party's pickup opportunities. A Republican-friendly 2026 Senate map and an unprecedented mid-decade GOP redistricting push further reduced the number of easy targets for Democrats.

Yet high prices, an unpopular war and Trump's falling approval ratings gave Democrats a chance to compete in places where they haven't prevailed in years — or, in some cases, decades.

Strong nominees went on to capitalize Tuesday night.

In Texas, Talarico, a 37-year-old state lawmaker and former seminarian, defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, a MAGA favorite with a controversial past. In Kansas, Hamilton, a 61-year-old megachurch pastor and former Republican, defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall. In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek, a state lawmaker and two-time Paralympic gold medalist who describes himself as a "prairie populist," defeated GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former local news anchor. In South Carolina, Andrews, a pediatrician, defeated incumbent Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after the recent death of her brother, longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted to book a return ticket to the U.S. Senate, where he previously served from 2007 to 2025.

Democrat Scott Colom was even leading incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi by a handful of votes.

These are not the types of races Democrats typically win. Trump won Ohio by 11 points in 2024. He won Iowa by 13 points. He won Texas by 14. He won Kansas by 16. He won South Carolina by 18. He won Mississippi by 24. He won North Carolina — where former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper breezed to victory — by 3.

Whether the 2026 results foreshadow some sort of larger rural realignment — or just a temporary rebuke of Trump's current policies — remains to be seen. But either way, Tuesday's blue tsunami swept well into red America.

Before Election Day, the president urged his supporters to vote like he was on the ballot. Afterward, he wrote on social media , "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

But preliminary exit polls suggested that even if Americans couldn't technically cast their votes for — or against — Trump this time around, his performance and policies were very much top of mind.

A full 62% of midterm voters said they disapproved of how Trump is handling his job as president. Just 38% said they approved. No recent president has emerged from a midterm election with an approval rating that low . Nearly 90% of voters said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote; about the same number said they were concerned about the price of gas and groceries. Nearly two-thirds said that Trump's policies, including tariffs, have made the U.S. economy worse and that going to war with Iran was the wrong decision. More than half said Trump is not a strong leader, does not fight for people like them, does not have the right priorities and does not have the mental capability to serve effectively as president.

Meanwhile, Trump did little to boost Republican chances on Election Day. His endorsements and interventions appeared to backfire in contest after contest . He attracted more attention in the closing days of the campaign for praising certain candidates' anatomy than for promoting his party's agenda. And he spent his final appearance before Nov. 3 talking about his troubled reflecting pool project .

Trump has defied history before. But in the end, 2026 seemed to show that even his powers have their limits. In 2006, President George W. Bush's Republicans lost both the House and the Senate after Americans soured on another Middle Eastern war. Something similar happened again on Tuesday.

The big story of the 2024 presidential election was how a rightward shift among previously left-leaning independents and Latinos helped propel Trump back to the presidency.

It appears both groups have shifted back.

According to Equis, a polling firm that focuses on Latino voters, Democrats increased their overall share of the Latino vote by 10 points in 2026 (65%) compared to 2024 (55%). In some states, like Virginia (+19 points) and New Jersey (+23 points), Democratic gains among Latinos were even bigger. In others, like Texas (60%) and Florida (56%), Democrats went from losing the Latino vote last time to winning it. Those gains likely contributed to key House victories in both states and major statewide wins in Texas.

As for self-identified independents, Trump split them about evenly with Democrat Kamala Harris two years ago . This time around, independents appear to have favored Democrats by roughly 17 percentage points .

For decades, Democrats have lamented their party's gerontocracy, from the Silent Generation stalwarts who long led their congressional caucus to the baby boomer candidates who seem to keep winning their presidential nominations.

But Tuesday's tsunami has provided the party with a whole new batch of " elder Millennial " stars, including Talarico (37), El-Sayed (42), Andrews (45), Turek (47), Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (44) and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (39), whose cruise to reelection has inspired buzz about a possible presidential bid (which he has publicly ruled out).

Before Nov. 3, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani were among the most prominent Democrats representing the party's next generation on the national stage. Now they have company.

articles.title: Democrat wins Texas railroad commissioner race after Republican faced backlash over racist comments
articles.summary: Democrat Jon Rosenthal has defeated GOP nominee Bo French, NBC News projects. French faced criticism from fellow Republicans for his inflammatory remarks.
articles.body: Democratic state Rep. Jon Rosenthal has won the race for Texas railroad commissioner, NBC News projects, defeating Republican Bo French, who faced widespread backlash in his own party and beyond for anti-immigrant, Islamophobic and antisemitic comments. Rosenthal will be one of three members of the Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates oil and gas production in the state. Members serve six-year terms. Rosenthal, a mechanical engineer, campaigned on a platform of lowering energy costs for Texans, implementing guardrails for data centers and weatherization requirements for gas production, and banning industry donations to commissioners. Follow live updates on the midterm elections He has served in the state House since 2019, representing the north-central region of Houston. Now, he joins a new slate of incoming Democratic officeholders, including Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa and Sen.-elect James Talarico. French, the former Tarrant County Republican Party chair, had a history of making discriminatory remarks, including one that made national news in the middle of the campaign. He drew significant criticism in September after he posted an image on X of students from the University of Texas, some of whom appeared to be South Asian or Indian. He wrote: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” Hours later, he reposted the same photo and cited it as an example showing that “Americans have been displaced by foreigners.” The remarks were met with strong condemnation from prominent Texas Republicans. Sen. John Cornyn said he wouldn’t vote for French. Karl Rove, the longtime GOP consultant and former adviser to President George W. Bush, said not only that he wouldn’t vote for French, but also that he would vote for Rosenthal, instead. Fort Worth Mayor Mattie Parker, another Republican, endorsed Rosenthal ahead of the election. “The Texas Railroad Commission is not a place for culture wars and bigotry — it’s the foundation of the Texas economy, and we cannot afford to hand it to the wrong leader,” Parker said in a statement shared by Rosenthal’s campaign. When French announced his bid for the statewide position, he said he was fighting back against Islam. In an appearance at the annual Conservative Political Action Conference, he said his party should embrace Islamophobia and deport 100 million people. “I’m going to say something that’s going to make some people uncomfortable: The problem is, we call it Sharia [law], but the problem is actually Islam,” French said, according to The Texas Tribune. “If they can infiltrate Texas and conquer Texas, then what’s going to happen? They’re going to be able to control the United States.” When French chaired the Tarrant County Republican Party, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, another fellow Republican, called on him to resign after he reportedly posted a poll online asking whether “Jews” or “Muslims” pose a bigger threat to the U.S. “Bo French’s words do not reflect my values nor the values of the Republican Party,” Patrick said on X. “Antisemitism and religious bigotry have no place in Texas.” Asked in an interview with WFAA-TV of Dallas in July whether he regretted the controversial comments against minority groups, French said he did not, adding, “Truth sounds like hate to those who hate the truth.”

articles.title: Dem wins Trump-targeted Texas district in rebuke of Republican redistricting shakeup
articles.summary: Johnny Garcia defeated Republican Carlos De La Cruz in Texas' redrawn 35th Congressional District, defying a Trump-backed redistricting map.
articles.body: Democrat Johnny Garcia is projected to win Texas' newly redrawn 35th Congressional District on Tuesday, overcoming a Republican-favored map designed to flip the seat after redistricting pushed Democratic Rep. Greg Casar into another district. Garcia, a Bexar County Sheriff's Deputy, defeated Republican candidate Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran who was backed by President Donald Trump. "Carlos De La Cruz just called and conceded the race, and I thanked him for a hard fought campaign," Garcia posted on X. "I'm grateful to the voters of TX-35 for their trust. Whether or not you voted for me, I'll fight to lower your costs, make healthcare affordable, and keep our community safe. Thank you to everyone who made this possible!" FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME The contest became a closely watched test of Texas Republicans' mid-decade redistricting strategy, which sought to strengthen the GOP's grip on the U.S. House ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Republican lawmakers dramatically reshaped the district in 2025 at President Donald Trump's urging, transforming a Democratic stronghold into territory that would have favored Trump by roughly 10 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. The overhaul also displaced the district's Democratic incumbent, Casar, who opted to seek election in the newly configured 37th Congressional District rather than defend his former seat. The new 35th District covers portions of San Antonio and surrounding communities in Bexar County and neighboring counties. The race pitted two candidates with sharply different backgrounds against one another. De La Cruz, a 20-year Air Force veteran and former gym owner, entered the general election with Trump's endorsement and a prominent family connection to Washington. His sister, GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz, represents Texas' 15th Congressional District. Garcia, a longtime Bexar County sheriff's deputy, campaigned as a moderate, law-and-order Democrat, emphasizing working families and household costs in his appeal to voters. Both candidates emerged from competitive May primary runoffs, with De La Cruz defeating Republican state Rep. John Lujan and Garcia overcoming Democratic rival Maureen Galindo. LATINO VOTERS SWING BACK TO DEMOCRATS AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS: POLL The district's Hispanic-majority electorate also placed the race at the center of a broader political question: whether Republicans could sustain Trump's 2024 gains among Hispanic voters in a midterm election without the president himself on the ballot. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The outcome carries implications beyond South Texas, offering a test of whether redistricting can translate favorable presidential voting patterns into congressional victories or whether candidate appeal and changing voter priorities can disrupt those calculations. articles.title: Idaho voters reject ballot measure on abortion, preserving the state’s ban, NBC News projects
articles.summary: The abortion ban went into effect in 2022 after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade.
articles.body: Voters have rejected an Idaho ballot measure that would have codified the right to an abortion up until fetal viability, NBC News projects. The move preserves Idaho’s abortion ban, which went into effect in 2022 following the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade, which had guaranteed abortion rights nationally. The Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act Initiative, also known as Proposition 1, would have gone into effect in 2027. Proposition 1 would have allowed the government to regulate abortion only after fetal viability, except in the case of a medical emergency to save the life of the woman. Follow live updates on the midterm elections The initiative defined fetal viability as a fetus’ having “a significant likelihood of sustained survival outside of the uterus without extraordinary medical measures.” Fetal viability is generally thought to be around six months into a pregnancy, or around 23 to 24 weeks. Proposition 1 stated that reproductive healthcare should be decided “by a person in consultation with their health care provider.” “The act supports a person’s right to reproductive freedom and privacy, protects the confidential nature of the patient-provider relationship, and secures a person’s right to make their own health care decisions without government interference,” it said. Proposition 1 would have given everyone in Idaho the right to “reproductive freedom and privacy,” which was defined as “the right to make personal decisions about reproductive health care that directly impact the person’s own body.” The initiative said Idahoans have a right to make their own decisions about abortion, childbirth care, contraception, fertility treatment, miscarriage care and prenatal, pregnancy and postpartum care. According to the Center for Reproductive Rights website, from 2022 to earlier this year, 11 states expanded access to abortion and reproductive care since the Supreme Court’s Dobbs decision. Almost a third of Idaho’s OB-GYNs moved away, stopped practicing or retired from August 2022 to December 2024, according to a study published in a medical journal.

articles.title: Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek wins re-election bid in Oregon
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Kotek defeated Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan in a rematch of their 2022 contest.
articles.body: Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek has won her re-election bid in Oregon, NBC News projects, defeating Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan. The contentious race was a rematch from 2022, when Kotek beat Drazan by just 4 points in the solidly Democratic state. Kotek was burdened by low approval ratings, with polls showing voters were concerned with cost-of-living issues as well as homelessness in the state. Drazan in particular criticized Kotek’s policies on taxes and data centers. According to a Pew Research Center study earlier this year, Oregon was among the top 10 states with the most planned data centers. In September, Kotek announced she would back a statewide moratorium on new data centers. Follow live updates on the midterm elections Meanwhile, Kotek sought to tie Drazan to President Donald Trump in a state he lost by 14 percentage points in 2024. “So Christine Drazan has said, ‘Take a risk, vote for me.’ But if we look at her voting record and we look at who she listens to, that would be a risk that I don’t think we should take as a state,” Kotek said during their first debate. “That risk would entail banning abortion, cutting the Oregon Health Plan, eliminating vote by mail, and when it comes to protecting our cities, when Oregon National Guard troops are deployed, no one would stand up for them.” Drazan tried to distance herself from Trump and instead focus on statewide issues, attempting to put pressure on Kotek over affordability. She said at a debate in October that Kotek “solves every single challenge that she sees, every single problem in the state of Oregon, with a new tax.” A Republican has not won a gubernatorial race in Oregon since 1982. Kotek became one of the first out lesbian governors in the country, along with Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, during the 2022 election. Prior to that, she had become the first out lesbian speaker of a state House in 2013.

articles.title: ‘Rejecting hate’: Abdul El-Sayed wins Senate seat despite racist attacks
articles.summary: The Democrat defeats Republican Mike Rogers to win Michigan seat to become first Muslim senator-elect in US history.
articles.body:
Detroit, Michigan — Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has defeated his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, to win the United States Senate seat in Michigan, overcoming a campaign of anti-Muslim attacks spearheaded by President Donald Trump.

With the victory on Tuesday, El-Sayed is set to become the first Muslim senator in US history. He will be sworn in on January 3 .

Maya Berry, executive director of the Arab American Institute (AAI), said Republicans had turned anti-Arab and anti-Muslim tropes into a pointed strategy against El-Sayed — one that eventually did not work.

“The electorate rejecting that bigotry is tremendous, I would argue, for every little boy named Abdul, every little girl named Zainab, every little kid named Bobby, because the reality is, at the end of the day, we’re talking about whether this country supports an inclusive democracy or not,” Berry told Al Jazeera.

After winning a hard-fought primary in August that saw the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spend more than $30m against him, El-Sayed, a critic of Israel’s policies, was subjected to an avalanche of unfounded accusations — including that he is a “jihadist” — by Trump and other Republicans.

El-Sayed, a former public health official, campaigned on expanding government-funded healthcare to all Americans, getting money out of politics, and addressing the affordability crisis.

The Democrat has also accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza and called for investing money currently spent on foreign wars to instead fix local issues.

The final days of the campaign were rocked by El-Sayed’s former primary opponent, Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens — a staunch Israel supporter — endorsing Rogers.

El-Sayed’s win helps Democrats regain control of the Senate, but for many of his supporters, it means far more than a single seat in the upper chamber of Congress.

Throughout Election Day on Tuesday, voters in Michigan told Al Jazeera the election could determine the direction of the state and the country for years to come.

For Democrats, the vote was about rejecting Trump’s agenda and defeating the racist rhetoric from the president and his allies.

Republicans not only used Islamophobia against El-Sayed, but also invoked Arab-Black tensions to try to peel off African American voters from the Democratic coalition.

Michigan is home to a large Arab American community.

Trump seized on that narrative, saying that any Black or Jewish person who backs El-Sayed is “crazy”.

But early election results show that El-Sayed performed well with Black voters in Detroit.

Gary Colbert, who was casting his ballot on the west side of Detroit, denounced Trump’s comment about Black voters.

“Everybody kind of knows he’s the true nut. He says any and everything,” Colbert told Al Jazeera.

Colbert — who lamented the rise in gas prices due to the Iran war — added that Trump and “his cronies” are negatively affecting people’s lives, “and they don’t care”.

Trump, who is struggling with low approval ratings, told supporters in Michigan last month to vote as if he was on the ballot.

On Tuesday, Frank Espinosa, a teacher who was volunteering at a voting station in Southwest Detroit — home to a large Latino community — said protecting immigrants from Trump’s crackdown is a priority for voters in the city in this election. The Trump administration has targeted immigrant communities across the country by deploying Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers on the streets, tasked with arresting allegedly undocumented migrants. Dozens of people have been shot, and several of them killed — including American citizens protesting against what they see as reckless methods of enforcement.

“I think the number one thing we want is ICE out of our streets,” Espinosa told Al Jazeera.

“We also want the end to foreign wars. I know my students want their gas bills to be better. We want affordability all across our city, not just at the gas pump, but at the grocery store as well.”

He added that the campaign targeting El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and Arab identity is “incredibly disheartening”.

“I also know that Detroit is better than all of that, and I think that there’s a lot of noise outside of our state, outside of our city. But here, I know Detroiters will ultimately do the right thing and ultimately vote Abdul for Senate,” Espinosa said.

In neighbouring Dearborn, a Detroit suburb known as the Capital of Arab America, the vote — for many — was about the right to belong to the US.

Ali Baleed Almaklani, a leader in the Yemeni American community, said the anti-Muslim campaign motivated the Arab and Muslim community to increase its political participation.

“We are sick and tired and the American people are generally sick and tired of all this hate,” Almaklani told Al Jazeera.

“He’s talking about healthcare, about the economy, about the issues that are hurting people, and on the other side all they talk about is ‘terrorism’ and baseless accusations about the Muslim Brotherhood.”

Dearborn saw a high voter turnout on Tuesday, with lines stretching across polling stations.

Several voters told Al Jazeera they are responding to bigotry through the ballot box.

In an animated, expletive-laden interview, Dearborn voter Mike Mohammed criticised the Republican-led campaigns to paint Arabs and Muslims, including El-Sayed, as foreigners.

“We’re more American than them. I’m more American than any of them m************. I grew up here. I went to this school,” he said, pointing to the elementary school where the voting was taking place.

Sally Howell, an emeritus history professor at the University of Michigan-Dearborn who pioneered academic research about Arab American communities, said El-Sayed’s victory shows that the American people want change.

“This change also includes a rejection of hate in politics, especially anti-Muslim hate,” Howell told Al Jazeera. “And it includes a recognition of the value of Palestinian lives alongside those of Americans, immigrants, and so many others. For the Arab community in Michigan, it means people can wake up in the morning knowing that their contributions to the American body politic will be acknowledged, their voices heard and welcomed, their labour rewarded.”

articles.title: Democrat Aaron Ford unseats GOP Gov. Joe Lombardo in Nevada
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Ford, Nevada’s attorney general, has flipped control of the governorship in the key battleground state.
articles.body: Nevada’s Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford has won the state’s gubernatorial race, NBC News projects, toppling Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. He will be the state’s first Black governor. Democrats sought to make the race a referendum on Lombardo’s and President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy. Ford and his allies blasted the “Lombardo-Trump economy,” with many of their attacks centered on the president’s 2025 tax cuts and spending bill, which Democrats warned would have devastating effects on poor Nevadans. They pointed to Trump’s tariffs as a particular sore spot in a state with an economy that relies heavily on tourism. And they attacked Lombardo over an agreement with the Trump administration this summer that could help ease the pathway for more data centers on public land there. That economic message hit hard in Nevada — a state where the rising costs of goods, gas, housing and healthcare weighed heavily on voters’ minds. Ford’s strategy was not unlike the one Lombardo employed to win the governor’s mansion in the first place, when he defeated Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak in 2022 by seizing on Nevadans’ economic frustrations and framing the election as a referendum on the sitting governor and his party’s policies in Washington. Lombardo attempted to walk a fine line on Trump in the battleground state. He appeared with Trump during a visit to Nevada this summer and celebrated policies like cutting taxes on tips. Even so, Lombardo quickly came out against some of Trump’s tariffs last year and highlighted other areas where he pushed back on Trump, including on solar power. And he sought to frame himself as doing what he could to help make life more affordable, while distancing himself from federal policies “I can’t control.” All the while, Lombardo used his past career in law enforcement in an effort to portray Democrats as weak on crime. But it wasn’t enough to insulate Lombardo in one of the most competitive states in the nation, where the last two governors failed to secure re-election. The result is a boon for Democrats two years ahead of the next presidential election. Nevada was one of the states where Trump allies sought to overturn Joe Biden’s victory by preparing alternate slates of presidential electors that falsely declared Trump the winner. Ford’s win also deals a blow to the GOP after the party’s successful gubernatorial campaign in 2022 and Trump’s 2024 victory.
