articles.title: LAURA INGRAHAM: Richer, safer and stronger: Why the Trump agenda deserves to keep going
articles.summary: Critics keep declaring Trumpism dead, but Laura Ingraham argues that the economic, geopolitical and cultural record tells a very different story about MAGA's durability.
articles.body: "This is the end of Trumpism!" "Conservative Populism, RIP." "Goodbye, MAGA!" If these pronouncements sound familiar, it’s because they are. The same people predicting this now in op-eds, online and in podcasts predicted the same after Trump’s first impeachment, after the 2020 election, after January 6, after the second impeachment and after every criminal indictment filed against him. Their wishful thinking is as dim-witted now as it was then. TRUMP HIGHLIGHTS THE 'POWER OF VETO' AS DEMS EXPECTED TO TAKE HOUSE, SENATE Any fair-minded political analyst would admit that over the past decade, Donald Trump has been the most consequential leader in the world, and that he has accomplished more than any Republican president in at least the past 100 years. His record should not be judged on midterm results but on what it has delivered. And if the question on the table is "Should Trump’s policies continue?" the record says yes — politically, economically, geopolitically and culturally. The political record Critics predicted Trump would destroy the Republican Party and set back American conservatism. The opposite happened. Across the West, the right has either collapsed or made its peace with the governing consensus. Canada hasn't had a conservative prime minister since 2015. Britain's Conservatives hold just 118 of 650 seats in the House of Commons. Marine Le Pen has never cleared 42% of the vote in a French presidential election. Germany's conservatives govern in coalition with the Social Democrats, and in Italy, The Economist recently praised Giorgia Meloni for "tacking to the middle." Only in America has the right governed on low taxes, lighter regulation, social conservatism and a strong military — and kept winning. Democrats had little trouble beating moderate Republicans like John McCain and Mitt Romney. Trump has confounded them for most of a decade. No other leader on the Western right can say that. The economic record We were told populism would wreck the economy. It hasn't. Trump worked with Congress to cut taxes and roll back regulation, and he has trimmed a bloated bureaucracy: Between December 2024 and June 2026, the federal workforce shrank by 255,000 employees, or 12%, according to The Washington Post. Ordinary families have benefited. Real median household income rose from $77,230 in 2016 to a record $87,460 last year, both measured in 2025 dollars. Those figures are adjusted for inflation and describe the household squarely in the middle. Nostalgia for the '80s and '90s is understandable, but the American middle class has never been richer than it is today. FOX NEWS POLL: COST-OF-LIVING CONCERNS WEIGH ON GOP IN MIDTERMS Inflation, the defining failure of the Biden years, has been tamed. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, peaked at 6.6% in September 2022 and was still 3.3% in November 2024. This September it stood at 2.6%. Headline inflation of 3.7% is in line with the eurozone's 3.8% and Britain's 3.5%. Americans are not uniquely squeezed. Freedom does not come cheap. Americans today are stronger, richer, safer and freer than we have been in decades, and those who want to see this country humbled, even humiliated, know it. Growth is outpacing our peers. In September, the OECD projected U.S. real GDP growth of 2.2% for 2026, the highest in the G7. The latest data are stronger still: the economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter, compared with 0.5% for the EU and roughly 1.3% for Canada. The upshot is that Americans are by far the wealthiest people of any major economy. The IMF projects 2026 GDP per capita of $95,212 in the United States, against $65,699 in Germany, $61,108 in Britain, $60,105 in Canada, $51,448 in France, $35,400 in Japan and $15,371 in China. The United States is not merely the richest major country on earth; it is pulling away from the rest of the West. The geopolitical record Critics warned that Trump's foreign policy would leave America isolated and weak. Instead, he is charting a course to victory over China, our only serious geopolitical rival. WHY TRUMP ZEROED IN ON GREENLAND, THE WORLD’S LARGEST ISLAND, MOSTLY COVERED IN ICE — IN 3 CHARTS Before Trump, Washington's establishment insisted that China's rise was good for America, a view the Obama administration voiced as late as 2012. Trump took a more realistic view. His tariffs kept state-subsidized Chinese cars from gutting our auto industry. His moves on the Panama Canal and Greenland denied Beijing footholds in our hemisphere. He is rebuilding a military that had grown dangerously weak and distracted by ideology. And our economic lead keeps widening: in 2016, U.S. GDP exceeded China's by $7.3 trillion; last year, the gap was $11.3 trillion. In the Middle East, Trump has severely degraded an Iranian military that threatened the entire region. Critics predicted the Strait of Hormuz would be closed. It hasn't been: The Wall Street Journal reports that Persian Gulf oil exports, counting both Hormuz shipments and alternative routes, now exceed prewar levels. All of this has been achieved without an invasion or boots on the ground. With a stronger military and a booming economy, American leverage abroad is likely the greatest it has been since the early 2000s. LIZ PEEK: GUARANTEED — DEMOCRAT MIDTERM WIN WOULD DELIVER CHAOS NOT 'AFFORDABILITY' The social record Some warned social conservatives that Trump didn't really share their priorities and that they would regret backing him. Consider what he delivered. For four decades, Republican leaders promised to do something about Roe v. Wade. Trump kept that promise, and Roe is gone. Unlike past Republican presidents, he has not appointed justices who drift left, and on most key constitutional questions the Supreme Court now has a solid conservative majority for the first time since the early 1930s. TRUMP DHS HITS 16 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH 0 RELEASES AT THE BORDER The border is closed to illegal immigration — another decades-old Republican promise that only Trump fulfilled. We were told this would devastate the economy. The data above say otherwise. What the Democrats are offering By any serious measure, the Trump movement ranks among the most successful in American history, and the country is better off for it — compared both with where we were and with our peers abroad. Tellingly, Democrats aren't seriously arguing that they would deliver a stronger economy, a firmer foreign policy or safer streets. Voters can see what their approach produces by looking at Canada and Western Europe. Instead, their campaign rests on a single promise: to go after Trump and everyone who has worked with him. It is a campaign of retribution, not prosperity. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Of course, voters, including this one, are frustrated with the Iran conflict, and they want lower gas prices. Others are simply tired of politics, and some may hope a Democratic win would at least bring some calm to America. But remember what President Reagan said: "Freedom is never more than one generation from extinction." Freedom does not come cheap. Americans today are stronger, richer, safer and freer than we have been in decades, and those who want to see this country humbled, even humiliated, know it. The socialists, Marxists and even run-of-the-mill Democrats did not run this year to make your life better. They ran to punish you for wanting more than the scraps the political establishment used to toss you. Do not fall for it. Can you imagine Republicans abandoning Reagan because he lost eight Senate seats in 1986? Did the Democrats abandon Obama after he lost nine Senate seats in 2014? Of course not. We know how Democrats almost destroyed America and what they intend to do to our Constitution if they get the chance. We may not have everything we want — we probably never will — but we have already made huge progress, and we just need to keep relentlessly fighting for the type of country we want. articles.title: Trump pledges to veto 'insane' Dem bills, pinpoints issue partially to blame for Republican losses
articles.summary: President Donald Trump blamed rising gas prices from the Iran conflict for GOP midterm losses, saying Americans backed the war but not the pain.
articles.body: President Donald Trump vowed to veto "insane" legislation from Democrats following the party's major midterm election victories Tuesday, while acknowledging that rising gasoline prices stemming from the conflict with Iran likely contributed to Republican losses. Trump, who posted an image of a red hat with the word "Veto" to Truth Social late Tuesday night, told Fox News Channel during live Election Night coverage that he was surprised by the GOP's performance but expressed confidence that he could work with Democrats despite their electoral gains. "They'll send over things that are insane and I'll veto them," Trump said. "And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll go out and they'll say, ‘How do we get this stuff done?’ And we'll work together." TRUMP CONGRATULATES DEMOCRATS AFTER DOMINANT MIDTERMS, SAYS HE LOOKS FORWARD TO WORKING WITH THEM Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, flipping at least seven Republican-held Senate seats and more than two dozen House districts. The sweeping victories dealt a major blow to Trump and the GOP, leaving Democrats positioned to block the president's legislative agenda, reject his nominees and launch investigations into his administration during his final two years in office. The president pointed to his veto authority as a negotiating tool and revealed that several Democratic lawmakers had already reached out to him. "You know, I have a lot of friends that are Democrats, believe it or not. I've already spoken to some of them," Trump said, adding that he had spoken with Democratic members of Congress, with others waiting to call. Trump also addressed the GOP's disappointing election-night performance, suggesting that Americans were reacting more to higher gasoline prices than to the military campaign against Iran itself. STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE "I don't think it's the war, Bret, I think it's the gasoline price," Trump told "Special Report" anchor Bret Baier. "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran, but they really probably weren't willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline." Trump defended his administration's actions against Iran, arguing that the economic consequences were temporary and necessary to achieve longer-term national security objectives. "I think a part of it was Iran. But at the same time, people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," Trump said. "I think historically it's going to be much more important than this evening, because you can't let the number one state sponsor of terror have a nuclear weapon." The president also blamed some Republican candidates for failing to energize his supporters, arguing that enthusiasm at his campaign rallies did not necessarily translate into votes for those he endorsed. "I'm a little bit surprised. I thought they'd do better," Trump said. "We had tremendous rallies. We had about 30 of them." Trump said some candidates had alienated his MAGA base by previously opposing him, while others simply failed to inspire voters to turn out. 'POD SAVE AMERICA' HOSTS CALL DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S MIDTERM WINS 'THE END OF THE TRUMP ERA' "They didn't like the candidates and some of the candidates that I endorsed fought me, and they didn't like that they fought me," Trump said. "And I wasn't on the ballot. If I was on the ballot, they would have gotten out," he added. Despite expressing disappointment over Republican losses, Trump praised Democrats for their performance while rejecting the suggestion that the results amounted to a personal defeat. "I think the Democrats did a good job, I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard," Trump said. articles.title: 5 key insights from the NBC News Exit Poll about the blue tsunami
articles.summary: Voters expressed feeling fed up with the economy; Democratic candidates emerged more well-liked and Trump was resoundingly rejected.
articles.body: It was a historic blue tsunami: The Democratic Party captured both chambers of Congress, flipping as many as seven seats in the Senate and at least 29 in the House of Representatives. Just two years ago, the nation had been hit by a red wave. How did things turn around so dramatically? A cocktail of crucial factors: Voters feeling fed up with the economy, Democratic candidates emerging as more well-liked, important voting blocs — including Latinos and Black men — shifting blue, opinions about the Republican Party dropping and a resounding rejection of President Donald Trump himself, according to the NBC News Exit Poll. Here are five key insights we have gleaned about Tuesday’s stunning midterms analyzing data from the poll, which surveyed more than 79,000 voters nationwide. Follow live updates on the midterm elections 1) Americans were deeply negative on the state of the economy and gloomy about the future of the country. An overwhelming majority of voters (75%) rated the nation’s economy as “not so good” or “poor,” the poll showed. And they soured on their trust in Republicans to handle it. Sixty-nine percent said the U.S. economic system favors the wealthy, and only 31% said it favors most Americans. This perception came at a time when the vast majority of voters expressed concerns about the cost of living. More than 80% of voters said they were worried about the price of necessities: gas and diesel fuel, food and groceries, utilities and healthcare. Thirty-seven percent of voters said they favored Republican control of the economy, while 43% favored Democrats — a flip in perspective from the 2024 election. Voters also blamed Trump: 65% said the president’s policies had made the economy worse. Just 27% said they had made the economy better. Sixty-two percent said higher-than-usual prices are more because of Trump’s policies than factors outside his control, and 65% said his tariff policies hurt the national economy. Their frustration extended beyond the economy — and into a pessimistic view of the U.S. overall. Three in four voters said they were unhappy with how things are going in the U.S., and more than a third (38%) said they were angry about the state of the country. More than half of voters (57%) said that life for the next generation of Americans will be worse than today; just 22% said they believed it would be better. 2) Democratic candidates enjoyed advantages on favorability, character and experience. In an overwhelmingly negative political environment, Democratic Senate candidates emerged as well-liked in races that looked tough for them at the beginning of the election cycle, according to the poll. Democrats above water on favorability included Jon Ossoff in Georgia, where a remarkable 59% of state voters said they viewed him favorably; James Talarico in Texas, where 52% of voters said they viewed him positively; and Josh Turek in Iowa, where 49% of voters said they viewed him favorably. All three candidates won their races. Republicans, meanwhile, struggled to win over voters. In two key Senate races, voters expressed negative opinions about Republican candidates’ personal character. In Kansas, 43% of voters said Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, an OB-GYN who faced scrutiny after The New York Times reported that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid bills, had the right character for the job. Marshall has described the story as a “hit job.” Voter opinions were worse about Ken Paxton’s personal character. Only 34% of Texas voters thought positively of the attorney general, who has battled scandals for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Republican controlled state House before the state Senate acquitted him. Both Paxton and Marshall lost their Senate bids. Candidates aligned with Trump also struggled. In North Carolina, Michael Whatley was seen as too supportive of Trump (60%), and in South Carolina, where the president endorsed Darline Graham, only 35% of voters said she had the right experience. 3) After flirting with the GOP in 2024, big Democratic voting blocs swung back with a vengeance. By ignoring or denigrating many of the new voters who were key to Trump’s victory two years ago, Republicans squandered the opportunity to cement a new coalition of voters. Latinos, who notably gave Trump almost half (46%) of their votes in 2024, bounced back to the Democrats, who garnered 62% of Latino support in races for the House, the poll showed. Among Black male voters, 1 in 5 went for Trump in 2024. That share shrunk to 13% for Republican House candidates this year. Trump narrowly won men under age 25 in 2024, getting 49% of their votes compared to 48% for Democrat Kamala Harris. But young men swung dramatically away from the GOP in House races this year: Democrats swept them by a 68% to 28% margin. On the whole, more Trump voters had buyer’s remorse (6% supported Democratic House candidates) than Harris voters (3% defected to the GOP). 4) And Trump himself was soundly rejected by voters. Trump tried to energize his base by encouraging his supporters to vote like, “I’m on the ballot.” But the nation had largely soured on his presidency, according to the poll. Trump’s approval rating among voters, just 38%, was the lowest Election Day rating for any president since 2008. Forty-three percent of voters said they cast their House ballot to express opposition to Trump. Just 16% said they voted to express support for him. Voters gave Trump overwhelmingly negative marks on key aspects of his presidency, saying that he prioritizes “his own personal interests” over the country’s (62%), that his war against Iran was the “wrong decision” (63%) and that his immigration actions had “gone too far” (57%). 5) A key distinction: It’s a blue tsunami, not a progressive earthquake. Politicians and pundits alike mistook Trump’s 2024 victory as an endorsement of his deeply conservative plans. But the 2024 NBC Exit Poll found little evidence of an ideological shift to the right. The story is the same this year: On key issues, voters are no more progressive than they were two years ago. Among voters this year, 64% said abortion should be legal in most or all cases. That’s just a notch below the share of 65% in 2024. Twenty-three percent of the electorate considered themselves liberal in 2024, while 35% called themselves conservative. Those numbers hardly budged among voters in 2026, standing at 25% liberal, 34% conservative. Voters’ opinions of socialism remained largely negative, at 54% unfavorable and 33% favorable. Just 1 in 5 voters this year considered themselves democratic socialists. By contrast, capitalism remains relatively well-regarded in the minds of voters (57% favorable, 32% unfavorable).

articles.title: Democrats win House, Senate in midterms landslide: Live updates
articles.summary: Democrats have won control of the House and Senate by grabbing dozens of seats from Republicans.
articles.body:
Some races remain too close to call, but voters have decisively handed control of Congress to Democrats, flipping dozens of seats from red to blue in a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump amid widespread anger over the cost of living and the war in Iran.

Democrats flipped at least seven seats in the Senate to gain a 54-seat majority in traditionally Republican states such as Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.

Adam Hamilton broke the longest Democratic drought in the country by becoming the first Democrat to win Kansas since 1932. James Talarico became the first Democrat to win a Texas Senate seat since 1988. Chris Pappas in New Hampshire became the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed beat his GOP opponent , becoming the nation's first Muslim U.S. senator.

Democrats celebrate blue tsunami. See the historic moment

Two Senate races − in Alaska and Mississippi − remain undecided. The Justice Department has appealed a lawsuit to investigate the Alaska results if the incumbent GOP Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan, loses by a small enough margin that a challenger with the same name made the difference.

Democrats flipped dozens of seats in the House of Representatives from California to New Jersey, including three seats in Iowa. Races in some western states remained too close to call early Wednesday.

Voters also elected governors in dozens of states. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa became the first Hispanic woman governor. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman governor. In Florida, Byron Donalds became the first Black Republican governor. And Democrat Xavier Becerra will become California's first Hispanic governor.

Talarico, Hinojosa celebrate victory at Texas staple Whataburger

11:04 AM ET, November 4 2026, Taylor Ardrey

Elected Texas officials James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa celebrated their victories at a state fast-food staple. Surrounded by cheering supporters at an Austin Whataburger on Tuesday, the 2026 midterm election winners were spotted smiling and clinking their soda cups.

"First stop post-win: Whataburger," Talarico , who defeated Republican Ken Paxton for U.S. Senate, wrote in an Instagram caption.

"We did it (Talarico)," and "For Texas," added Hinojosa , who beat incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott .

Vice President JD Vance: 'The reason we lost is the war'

10:59 AM ET, November 4 2026, Miles J. Herszenhorn

Vice President JD Vance blamed election night's stunning Republican wipeout on the war against Iran, which upended the global economy and drove up fuel prices across the country.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote in a post on X . "The president himself said so last night."

The war in the Middle East, which started eight months ago when the U.S. and Israel launched a joint attack against Iran, was deeply unpopular among American voters. Republican candidates paid a steep prices at the polls, losing Senate races in deep-red states such as South Carolina, Texas, and Kansas.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

"But everyone knows why we lost," he added. "And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

Mike Johnson won't seek House leadership role

10:52 AM ET, November 4 2026, Zachary Schermele and Francesca Chambers

House Speaker Mike Johnson told staff on Wednesday morning that he would not run for minority leader after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections, two sources familiar with the announcement said.

Johnson handily won reelection to his Louisiana congressional district. But members of his party lost across the country on an election night that will put Democrats in the majority in the House and Senate in the next legislative session.

Tejano star Bobby Pulido flips Republican congressional seat in key Texas race

10:27 AM ET, November 4 2026, Melissa Montoya

The Texas musician who campaigned at concerts and quinceañeras as a "conservative Democrat" just flipped a key congressional seat in Texas.

Bobby Pulido , the Tejano star from South Texas, unseated U.S. Rep. Monica De La Cruz on Tuesday in the state's 15th Congressional District, a former Democratic stronghold the party lost due to a shift to the right by Latino voters in 2022.

Pulido, 53, won the Rio Grande Valley district, east of San Antonio, by a sizable margin after campaigning on affordability, health care, getting corporate money out of elections and the negative impacts of Trump's mass deportation raids, while distancing himself from the national Democratic Party on other border policy and culture war issues. "I'm not team red. I'm not team blue. I'm team you," he often told voters.

"Thank you South Texas, tonight we made history," the congressman-elect said in a written statement late Tuesday. "For over 30 years, you played my music at your weddings, your quinceañeras, and your carne asadas, and the past year you welcomed me into those same celebrations on the campaign trail. Tonight, you trusted me with something even bigger than a song, you trusted me with your future and I will work hard everyday to honor it."

Dow soars more than 1,100 points as Dems flip Congress

10:07 AM ET, November 4 2026, Kim Hjelmgaard

The Dow and other U.S. benchmark stock indexes soared higher as investors reflected on a power shift in Washington that saw Democrats regain control of both chambers of Congress.

The Dow jumped more than a 1,100 points in early trading, according to Bloomberg market data. That's a rise of more than 2%. There were also strong gains for the S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq indexes.

Economists at RaboResearch Global Economics & Markets said in an investor note on Nov. 4 that as general rule of thumb asset prices tend to favor administrations with "right of center" policies.

However, they noted that the positive moves may have been triggered by conciliatory comments from President Donald Trump willing to work with Democrats in Congress.

Mike Johnson: 'A new battle is just beginning'

09:38 AM ET, November 4 2026, Christopher Cann

House Speaker Mike Johnson in a statement overnight acknowledged a seismic defeat for the GOP, writing "while the outcome of this midterm is not what we'd hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning."

"Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world," he wrote on X .

"We will continue pressing forward with our agenda of common sense, and our vision to make America great again—and come 2028, we WILL take back the House and we will finish the job," he added.

With Democrats in control, will life get more affordable?

09:17 AM ET, November 4 2026, Rachel Barber

Exit polls revealed Americans' frustration over high prices helped deliver key victories for Democratic candidates, many of whom pledged to lower the cost of living on the campaign trail.

But experts say voters should mellow their expectations. Even if Democrats control Congress, they'll have to get legislation signed by President Donald Trump, or "Mr. Veto" as he nicknamed himself in an interview with the New York Post.

Several factors are contributing to the United States' stubborn inflation, including the Iran war, tariffs, and the AI buildout.

"The extent to which the new Congress will be able to substantially revert any of those causes seems to be quite low," Francesco D'Acunto, an associate professor of finance at Georgetown University, said.

However, he said that after a massive blue wave, Trump and Republicans may be more likely to work with Democrats on proposals to make housing more affordable and lower healthcare costs — things that would benefit constituents of lawmakers from both parties. He added that Democratic wins on the state level may also slow the AI buildout, which is pushing up prices in select categories.

"Voters would expect, given this big sort of change in Congress, everything will suddenly and immediately change," D'Acunto said. "Voters have to be patient to see that the effects on inflation and prices might be slower than they might expect."

Midterms mark historic firsts across race, gender, religion and sexual orientation

09:13 AM ET, November 4 2026, Swapna Venugopal Ramaswamy

Along with historic breakthroughs for Black candidates, the 2026 midterms also saw several other firsts, smashing political glass ceilings around gender, religion, race and sexual orientation.

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim to be elected to the U.S. Senate, defeating Republican Mike Rogers. He was called a "jihadist" by President Donald Trump during the campaign.

Democrat Xavier Becerra made history after being elected as California's first Hispanic governor. A son of Mexican immigrants, he will govern a state where Hispanics make up more than 40% of the population .

Texas Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa became the first Hispanic governor to be elected in the Lone Star state, and the first Democratic governor in more than three decades.

Democrat Deb Haaland of New Mexico made history after being elected the first Native American woman to serve as a governor of any state. She previously made history as the first Native American woman in Congress and the first Native American woman in the Biden administration cabinet.

Florida Democrat Pia Dandiya notched a historic first after becoming the first Indian American to be elected to Congress in the Sunshine state.

In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, won the race to become the first Native American woman in the Senate.

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man to serve in the U.S. Senate after defeating former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu for New Hampshire's open Senate seat. He will become one of two openly LGBTQ+ members in the Senate, joining Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin, who is a lesbian.

Michigan elected Jeremy Moss to the U.S. House of Representatives, winning the race to become the state's first openly gay member of Congress.

Democrat Amy Acton become Ohio's first female governor after defeating Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who ran a controversial campaign ad featuring Acton's estranged birth mother criticizing Acton.

09:01 AM ET, November 4 2026, Melina Khan

Former President Barack Obama said Americans sent a "clear message" in midterm elections with Democrats' commanding landslide.

"Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face," he said in a social media statement .

He urged leaders to continue riding the blue wave into the next two years.

"While this administration has another two years in office, our job now is to roll up our sleeves, make changes wherever we have the power to do so, prevent further damage, and lay the groundwork for the future," he said.

Obama returned to the campaign trail in recent weeks, backing candidates including Abdul El-Sayed , Amy Acton and Keisha Lance Bottoms . He made headlines for likening the White House decor to that of a Cheesecake Factory and even throwing out a rare mention of his tan suit controversy.

Jimmy Kimmel mocks Trump after midterm elections: 'Red wedding'

08:58 AM ET, November 4 2026, Brendan Morrow

Jimmy Kimmel celebrated the results of the midterm elections on his Tuesday show. "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" was taped while midterm election results were still coming in, but late enough for it to be clear that what the late-night comedian dubbed a "blue tsunami" was occurring.

"Democrats have officially taken the House thanks to President Trump," Kimmel said. "Blob Vila flipped another house. The blue wave made landfall, and now, the red wedding begins. The bad news is, I guess we're not getting that $5,000 ."

In his monologue, Kimmel argued things didn't go Trump's way in the midterms because the president's priorities "are insane" and "have no relation to what Americans are worried about." To make that point, on one side of the screen behind him, he showed a list of issues Americans are concerned about, including inflation, war, health care and housing. On the other side, Kimmel put up a list of issues that "MAGA seems to be worried about," including "transgender" and "Black Helen of Troy," the latter referring to Lupita Nyong'o's casting in "The Odyssey ."

Chris Christie condemns Vivek Ramaswamy and JD Vance after Ohio loss

08:46 AM ET, November 4 2026, Erin Mansfield

In a viral moment on ABC News, former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie condemned Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who lost the race for governor of Ohio on Tuesday, and Vice President JD Vance, who campaigned for Ramaswamy even as other Republicans distanced themselves.

Christie's criticism centered on Ramaswamy's campaign ad that featured Democratic opponent Amy Acton's estranged mother, who was reportedly living in a car at the time the video was shot. The two women had been estranged for nearly 50 years following the mother's husband being charged with sexually abusing Acton as a child.

"Vivek Ramaswamy will be forgotten," Christie said. "He is going to be sent to the dustbin of history. But JD Vance is going to be remembered, I think, from this campaign, for more than anything else ... that he stood by that ad. A man who wrote a book on Catholicism stood behind that ad. It's a disgrace."

Historic wins for Black candidates in midterms

07:52 AM ET, November 4 2026, Swapna Venugopal Ramaswamy

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) will become the first Black Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives after a sweeping Democratic win. As speaker, Jeffries would be second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms , the former mayor of Atlanta, became the first Black female governor in the country's history.

Byron Donalds, the Republican congressman from Florida, will become the first Black governor from the state.

Democrat David Crowley won Wisconsin's governor race, becoming the first Black person to hold the office.

With Illinois Lt. Governor Juliana Stratton winning her race for the U.S. Senate in the state, three Black women will serve simultaneously in the U.S. Senate for the first time in history. Stratton will join Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland. All three are Democrats.

How sports figures fared in the elections

07:51 AM ET, November 4 2026, Elizabeth Flores

The 2026 midterm elections saw several former sports figures step into the political arena, with some achieving notable victories while others fell short of their goals.

Former NFL player Colin Allred, a Democrat who played four seasons with the Tennessee Titans before a neck injury in 2010 ended his football career, went on to earn a law degree and enter public service. In Texas, Allred secured a resounding victory, winning re-election to the U.S. House of Representatives by defeating Republican Patrick Gillespie.

Joining Allred in the House is former MLB player Mark Teixeira, a Republican, who will succeed Rep. Chip Roy after narrowly defeating Democrat Kristin Hook in a closely contested race. Teixeira had a 14-year MLB career, playing for the Texas Rangers, Atlanta Braves, Los Angeles Angels and New York Yankees, and winning a World Series with the Yankees in 2009. Read more .

Rep. Lauren Boebert trails in uncalled race

07:46 AM ET, November 4 2026, Erin Mansfield

Republican firebrand Lauren Boebert is trailing in the vote count in her attempt at a fourth term in Congress, even though election analysts and news organizations have not called the final outcome of the race.

Democrat Eileen Laubacher has 49.2% of the votes in Colorado's 4th Congressional District, and Boebert has 47.7%, with 83% of the votes counted, according to the Associated Press.

Mississippi Senate race still too close to call

07:17 AM ET, November 4 2026, Erin Mansfield

Major news outlets and election analysts have yet to call the race for U.S. Senate in Mississippi, where Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is trying to fend off Democratic challenger Scott Colom.

Results at 3:48 a.m. showed Colom ahead of Hyde-Smith by 43 votes with 96% of votes counted, according to the Associated Press. Several counties in northeast Mississippi show only 90% of votes have been counted.

articles.title: America saw the blue wave coming — but drastically underestimated the extent of the Dem tsunami
articles.summary: James Talarico toppled Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa unseated Greg Abbott as Texas delivered historic Democratic upsets in the 2026 midterms.
articles.body: Polling and election analysts pointed to Democratic gains in the 2026 midterms, but the results brought wider margins and bigger upsets that even some of the most ambitious predictions didn't see coming. This included a historic Democratic breakthrough in Texas and other deep red strongholds. Democrats won control of the Senate and House in Tuesday's election in what could be their largest House majority in nearly two decades. The results marked a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump, who ran in 2024 on fixing the economy and ending all wars. He launched a campaign blitz in the final weeks of the campaign cycle to rally Republican voters — but it wasn't enough to save the party's floundering message. DEEP IN TRUMP COUNTRY, A NEW GENERATION REVEALS THE DIVIDE BEHIND TEXAS’ TIGHT SENATE RACE That rejection was especially striking in Texas, where Democrats pulled off twin upsets, with James Talarico defeating Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gina Hinojosa unseating Gov. Greg Abbott. The victories defied expectations in a state Trump carried by double digits just two years earlier. A Fox News poll in October showed Talarico and Paxton nearly tied, with Abbott leading Hinojosa. Both Democrats ultimately won by wide margins. The Texas Senate race was marked as a "toss-up" by the bipartisan Cook Political Report that gave Republicans an advantage with an R+6 ranking. But as of the early morning hours of Wednesday, Talarico held 53.9% of the vote to Paxton's 44.2% — a 9.7% gap in a race where polls were showing a clean match-up. Abbott's race was the biggest miss when it came to ratings and polling versus real results. Hinojosa flew mostly under the radar, with Cook ranking the race a "lean Republican" — but the Democrat candidate ran away with a nearly 7% victory gap as of 3 a.m. on Wednesday. And the Texas results came amid a broader Democratic tsunami. Texas’ Democratic upsets came as voters nationwide voiced dissatisfaction with Trump and the economy. A Fox News poll found Trump’s approval at 36%, while 74% of voters rated the economy negatively. POLL FLASHES WARNING SIGNS FOR REPUBLICANS IN 7 BATTLEGROUND SENATE RACES Democrats’ sweeping gains extended beyond Texas, with Senate upsets in Kansas and South Carolina, two states Trump carried by double digits in 2024. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton scored a historic defeat over Sen. Roger Marshall, ending Republicans’ 94-year winning streak in Senate races in the state. Kansas will send to the U.S. Senate their first Democrat elected senator in nearly a century. While the race was ranked a "toss-up," it still marks a historic departure for the ruby-red state. And in deep red South Carolina, Annie Andrews defeated Sen. Darline Graham, who had been appointed to succeed her late brother, Lindsey Graham, but couldn't secure a victory at the ballot box. The race was ranked "lean Republican," but the divide was 4.2 points as of Wednesday morning, marking a significant upset and an end to the more than two-decade reign of Grahams' holding onto the South Carolina Senate seat after Lindsey was first elected in 2002. While Maine has long been considered a purple state, its 30-year-tenured Republican Senator, Susan Collins, was ousted in Tuesday's midterm by Democrat Troy Jackson. Collins was widely viewed as a career politician and served five terms in the U.S. Senate. Cook rated the race a "toss-up," but the 6-point divide was still viewed as a major political upset. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Taken together, the results showed that the Democratic wave reached well beyond the usual battlegrounds, sweeping into states and seats that Republicans had long counted on carrying.

articles.title: Collins concedes U.S. Senate race to Jackson
articles.summary: (The Center Square) — Incumbent Sen. Susan Collins was edged out by Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in a major upset that helped his party win control of...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) — Incumbent Sen. Susan Collins was edged out by Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in a major upset that helped his party win control of the U.S. Senate in Tuesday's midterms.

Collins reportedly called Jackson around midnight Tuesday to congratulate him with the latest results showing Jackson with a 52% to Collins 47% in preliminary voting returns. The Associated Press hadn't yet called the race.

"It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate," Collins, a five term senator, said in the statement. "I'm proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years. I called Troy Jackson tonight to congratulate him and to assure him that my staff and I will work to ensure a smooth transition."

Jackson, a former state Senate President, posted a brief statement on social media thanking voters and pledging to work "to build a government that works for all of us."

"Maine, I owe you everything," he posted on X. "I'm ready to get to work for Mainers in the U.S. Senate, and I promise you this: I'll never forget where I came from or who I'm fighting for. Thank you."

The Senate race was considered a must-win contest Tuesday for the Democratic Party as it pushes to retake the U.S. Senate, where Republicans currently have a 53-45 majority.

It has been the focus of national attention since the Democrat Party's first nominee, Graham Platner, was forced to bow out of the race earlier this year amid sexual harassment and assault claims.

The latest polling has shown a tight race between Collins and Jackson, who has led in recent surveys, but within the margin of error. The Cook Political Report had rated the Senate race a "toss up."

Jackson, an Allagash logger, replaced Platner as the party's nominee at a hastily organized special convention. He has run as a progressive candidate with backing from Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, both of whom visited the state last month to stump for his campaign.

Collins, a moderate, is the only Republican senator running for reelection this year in a Democratic-led state that Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 presidential election.

On the campaign trail, she stressed her record as a moderate and for bucking President Trump on tariffs, immigration enforcement, and other key issues.

But Jackson sought to tie Collins to Trump's unpopular policies, and has criticized her votes that led to the confirmation of conservative U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who later voted to overturn federal abortion protections.

Democrats and Republicans have pumped tens of millions of dollars into a crush of TV and digital advertising into Maine to sway undecided voters ahead of the election.

Voter turnout in the state was expected to be high, driven in part by the wide-open gubernatorial and congressional races. More than 275,000 ballots were cast during Maine's nearly month-long early voting period, but the overall turnout won't be known for days. Under state law, absentee ballots cast by mail must be returned to local election clerks by 8 p.m. Tuesday to be counted.

articles.title: America is heading for two years of constitutional brinkmanship
articles.summary: An unlikely mix of political bargains and constitutional confrontation will define the next two years.
articles.body:
To understand the coming collision between President Donald Trump and a Democratic Congress, one must first discard the textbook formulas of US governance. The United States is about to witness a political experiment for which there is no modern precedent: a purely transactional populist, entirely unmoored from traditional ideological orthodoxy, forced to share power with a legislative branch unified in partisan hostility.

The conventional wisdom predicts immediate, paralysing gridlock. That is a misreading of the terrain. Trump does not view politics through the lens of conservative dogma or constitutional restraint; he views it through the lens of the deal. Consequently, his governance will not be characterised by passive stagnation, but by an aggressive, volatile mix of transactional bipartisanship and raw executive unilateralism.

Domestically, the ideological lines will blur. For decades, the Republican Party was defined by its commitment to limited government and free markets. Trump has spent a decade dismantling that consensus. Confronted with a Democratic House of Representatives and a Democratic Senate, he will feel no tribal loyalty to standard conservative policy. Instead, expect him to seek out areas of populist overlap.

When it comes to massive infrastructure spending, protectionist trade policy and aggressive state intervention to protect domestic manufacturing, Trump is often closer to the Democratic centre-left than to the ghost of former President Ronald Reagan. He will dare the opposition majorities to vote against legislation that pours millions of dollars into their districts or levies tariffs that protect their blue-collar constituents. It will be an unholy, ad hoc alliance — issue-by-issue, fleeting, and transactional — designed to deliver the optics of victory for both a populist president and a vulnerable congressional majority.

Where such transactions fail, however, the venue will shift from the legislative chamber to the administrative state controlled by the executive. Trump will not accept the traditional boundaries of a divided government. If necessary, he will govern by decree. Executive orders, emergency declarations and expansive interpretations of federal statutes will be deployed to bypass a stubborn Capitol Hill. The administration will dare the Democratic leadership to tie up the government in the federal courts, turning the slow wheels of the judiciary into a political weapon.

Yet, the true test of this fragile constitutional architecture will not occur on the domestic stage. It will happen abroad, specifically in the volatile expanses of the Middle East, where the executive branch enjoys its greatest constitutional latitude.

The immediate flashpoint is Iran. The Trump doctrine rests on a foundation of maximum economic pressure backed by highly unpredictable, asymmetric tactical deterrence. It is a posture designed to keep adversaries off balance. But a Democratic Congress, historically wedded to the framework of multilateral diplomacy and deeply wary of congressionally unauthorised foreign entanglements, will view this unpredictability not as a strategic asset but as an existential danger.

The US is likely headed for a historic constitutional showdown over the War Powers Resolution of 1973. Democratic majorities will also aggressively use the power of the purse to place statutory fences around the commander-in-chief, attempting to defund military manoeuvres or explicitly prohibit unilateral escalations against Tehran. Trump will treat these attempts at legislative constraints with open contempt. Asserting an absolute, almost unrestrained reading of the Constitution’s Article II executive authority, the president will argue that modern geopolitical threats require executive agility, not governance by congressional committee. When the rockets fly, the president will act unilaterally, leaving Congress to meaningless academic debates.

Hanging over this entire drama is the ultimate constitutional weapon: the threat of impeachment by Congress. In a Washington where both the House and the Senate are controlled by the president’s opponents, oversight will cease to be an instrument of governance and become an engine of partisan political destruction.

Democratic congressional committee chairs will launch a relentless, multifront campaign of subpoenas and investigations. Every member of Trump’s cabinet will live in a permanent state of interrogation; every foreign policy decision will be audited for high crimes and misdemeanours. The House will almost certainly draft articles of impeachment, not as an extraordinary remedy for rare misconduct, but as a routine penalty for political nonconformity.

Yet, this strategy carries severe risks for the opposition. Trump does not fear institutional warfare; he thrives on it. He will transform the spectacle of congressional investigations into the theatre of public grievance. To his base, a hostile Congress will be framed not as a coequal branch of government performing its constitutional duty, but as an illegitimate, obstructionist cabal subverting the will of the forgotten American voter.

Because the structural math of the Senate requires a two-thirds majority for removal of the president, actual eviction from the Oval Office remains a statistical fantasy. Impeachment will therefore achieve not displacement, but a permanent state of institutional friction.

What the US is about to enter is not two years of legislative inactivity, but a phase of perpetual brinkmanship. It will be an era in which governance occurs only in the narrow, volatile intervals between constitutional crises. The US system was built to withstand institutional tension, but it also requires a basic reverence for institutional boundaries to function. With a transactional populist president in the White House and an adversarial army on Capitol Hill, those boundaries will be tested as never before. The architecture will hold, but the foundation will shake.

articles.title: Can Democrats stop Iran war, reverse Trump’s tariffs after midterms win?
articles.summary: Democrats can block Trump’s legislative agenda, launch investigations but don’t have the numbers to override his veto.
articles.body:
Democrats have taken control of the United States House of Representatives and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections in a scathing defeat for US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.

The Congress that will convene in early January will be radically different from the first two years of Trump’s second presidential term, which saw Republicans holding majorities in both chambers.

While Democrats will have greater power to scrutinise Trump’s policies and obstruct any legislation they oppose, there is still a lot a president can do without congressional approval.

Here is a look at some pressing political issues and how a Democratic majority in both chambers might affect them:

Trump has acknowledged the role the war on Iran has played in Republican losses in the midterm elections. “I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time, people understood the importance of what I’ve done with Iran,” Trump said during a telephone interview with Fox News.

Frustration among voters about inflation, and the rising cost of fuel and groceries have been among the main factors behind their rebuke to Republicans. Democrats tapped into this by campaigning heavily on affordability and domestic spending.

Trump embarked on the war on Iran with Israel in February without congressional authorisation. He could still order attacks, but he could also face constraints from the new Congress. Lawmakers could use their power to deny additional funding when the current government-funding bill expires on December 11, presenting a critical budget constraint on Trump’s military decisions.

However, James Boys, research fellow at the Centre on US Politics at University College London, said that while Congress may wish to cut off funding, it may not be straightforward. “With troops in theatre, this would prove to be highly problematic and be seen to be placing American lives at risk,” he said.

Analysts also said the War Powers Resolution is unlikely to succeed in reining Trump in. Previous attempts to use the 1973 federal law have been defeated or rendered ineffective.

The War Powers Resolution states that a president can repel an imminent attack, but military actions must end within 60 days unless Congress declares war. The president can then issue a veto, which can only be overcome by a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and Senate.

The projected breakdown of the newly elected Congress shows that Democrats are well short of those supermajority thresholds.

Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the UCD Clinton Institute in Dublin, Ireland, said that while Congress is constrained without a two-thirds majority, what it could do is propose legislation by “working with some Republicans who might distance themselves from Trump” after the resounding declaration of dissatisfaction voters have given the president in these midterm elections.

For example, he said, “JD Vance, the vice president, opposed the war and has done so from the start.” Last week, Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief in a reported effort to revive talks and avert further attacks.

“[Will] he now push even harder to end the war?” Lucas asked.

However, Boys said the fact that Trump no longer faces election himself because the US Constitution requires him to leave office at the end of his second term may make the president instead feel that “he is now unleashed to act with impunity on the world stage”.

“Indeed, given his weakened domestic political circumstances, one can easily imagine Donald Trump escalating policies in the Middle East as he seeks to establish an indisputable presidential legacy,” he added.

Last year, Trump unleashed tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on about 90 countries with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. The move, which rattled global markets, was struck down by the Supreme Court in February, but the Trump administration has found workarounds to that ruling.

Days after the Supreme Court’s 6-3 vote, Trump doubled down on the tariffs, quickly signing an executive order based on a different statute and raising them from 10 percent to 15 percent. However, those tariffs are limited to 150 days unless they are extended by Congress.

Democrats have blamed Trump’s tariffs for exacerbating the rising cost-of-living crisis as tariffs ultimately fall back on US importers who pass them on to consumers. They accused Trump of “pickpocketing the American people”. A Democratic-controlled Congress could push for exceptions that would give exporters some temporary relief, but any deeper shift in US trade policy will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election and the new occupant of the White House.

Boys said the “situation regarding tariffs remains before the United States courts” and whether the government must give back tariff money it has already collected – and exactly how much of it – remains in dispute.

The one area in which Congress is expected to follow through regardless of the flip in party control is in passing tougher restrictions on China’s access to technology. These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology, and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence chips remain in authorised locations to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries.

Lucas said one major outcome of the midterm vote is that Democrats will now assume the chairmanships of all congressional committees, which have the power to launch investigations and subpoena witnesses.

This could result in scrutiny of the Trump family’s vast business empire, the president’s ties with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s handling of the war with Iran. They could even try to impeach Trump for a third time over the conflict.

Congress also may – and plans to – launch extensive investigations into the Trump administration’s immigration policies. Democrats have repeatedly advocated for using their new subpoena power to scrutinise collaboration between the US tax agency, the Internal Revenue Service, and the Department of Homeland Security on the Trump administration’s policy of deporting refugees and migrants.

Detaining people at airports and hearings in their immigration cases became part of Trump’s efforts to carry out mass deportations – one of his 2024 campaign promises . In the lead-up to Tuesday’s elections, Fox News released a poll that found 53 percent of registered voters felt the immigration crackdown had “gone too far”.

The Homeland Security Department has argued that about 70 percent of its immigration detainees are criminals, if pending charges are factored in. But critics have questioned that statistic, given that the legal system in the US gives suspects the presumption of innocence until they are proven guilty in a court of law.

Lucas said the midterm vote means “Democrats and responsible Republicans can now reach out to the state and local communities and encourage them to pursue recovery and responsible policies.”

articles.title: Meet the far-left socialists coming to Congress next year
articles.summary: House Democrats will see a slew of new far-left lawmakers enter their ranks next year after Tuesday night's midterm elections.
articles.body: As House Democratic leaders prepare to take the reins of power in Congress, they are also poised to reckon with far-left rebels who could make their lives difficult over the next two years. Democrats are projected to win back the House majority after Tuesday night’s midterm elections. It comes after a far-left insurgency roiled Democrats' primary elections, and some of those socialist candidates are now expected to be heading to Capitol Hill next year. RISING SOCIALIST STARS ON TRACK TO CONGRESS: WHO ARE DARIALIZA AVILA CHEVALIER, BRAD LANDER AND CLAIRE VALDEZ? Darializa Avila Chevalier, New York Darializa Avila Chevalier is projected to be the next House representative from New York's 13th congressional district, which covers Upper Manhattan and parts of the Bronx. Chevalier's victory comes after she scored an upset victory over Congressional Hispanic Caucus Chairman Rep. Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y., amid an anti-incumbent wave that swept Empire State elections. Born in Florida to immigrant parents from the Dominican Republic, she moved to New York City to attend Columbia University for her undergraduate degree. Chevalier has already earned criticism from her future Republican colleagues for past comments, including a now-deleted post on X, then Twitter, where she purportedly wrote, "I forgot to get napkins so I just wiped my hand on the American flag behind me." She's notably withheld support from Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., to be the next speaker of the House, telling Vanity Fair she would need certain "commitments" on progressive issues like Medicare for All. JEFFRIES WELCOMES DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS INTO THE FOLD AS CRITICS WARN PARTY IS REVEALING 'EXACTLY WHO IT IS' Claire Valdez, New York Claire Valdez is another member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) who scored an upset victory during New York's primaries, defeating a Democrat backed by retiring Rep. Nydia Velázquez, D-N.Y., for the party's nomination. MAMDANI-BACKED SOCIALIST WINS IN NEW YORK EXPOSE GROWING RIFT BETWEEN DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT, INSURGENT LEFT Valdez is now projected to take over Velázquez's seat in New York's 7th congressional district, which includes parts of Brooklyn and Queens. Valdez is currently a member of the New York State Assembly. On her campaign website, she touts herself as a "dual citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation and the United States." She also has not confirmed whether she will support Jeffries for speaker, telling New York Magazine she would not "negotiate in public" but that she would "see how the midterms shake out." CARVILLE WARNS DEMOCRATS MAY NEED TO BLOCK FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES FROM JOINING CAUCUS, MODERATE GROUP DISAGREES Donavan McKinney, Michigan Donavan McKinney in Michigan's 13th congressional district is another beneficiary of the anti-incumbency backlash during the 2026 election cycle. He's now projected to come to Congress after earlier defeating Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., in the primaries. McKinney is a DSA member and was backed by other prominent socialists like Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich. The district he is poised to represent includes part of Detroit and its suburbs. He recently told Jacobin Magazine that his biggest policy goals include Medicare for All, universal childcare and getting corporate money out of elections. Also in the interview, he accused his primary opponent of having taken campaign cash from Immigration and Customs Enforcement contractors, the pro-Israel lobby and other corporate interests. Israel had been the defining issue in his primary campaign. Thanedar was a former DSA member who left the organization over members' celebrations of the Oct. 7 terror attack by Hamas. DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT Melat Kiros, Colorado Melat Kiros is a DSA member and former attorney whose upset victory in Colorado's 1st congressional district is forcing an end to longtime Rep. Diana DeGette's political career. DeGette, D-Colo., a progressive who has been in Congress since 1997, lost her Denver-area seat in a shocking primary loss to Kiros, a 29-year-old political newcomer. Kiros was born in Ethiopia "just weeks before her father was selected by the United States' Diversity Visa Lottery," according to her campaign website. She's drawn controversy for her fierce anti-Israel stance, which includes calling the Oct. 7 terror attack by Hamas an "inevitable" result of the Jewish country's own actions, according to multiple reports. She has also opposed its existence as a Jewish state. Kiros is also among those who will not commit to supporting Jeffries for speaker. GOP LAWMAKER URGES JOHNSON TO SCRUTINIZE NEW SOCIALIST LAWMAKERS' 'ACCESS TO INTELLIGENCE' Chris Rabb, Pennsylvania Pennsylvania state lawmaker Chris Rabb is poised to enter the House of Representatives to represent the state's 3rd congressional district next year. The Democratic socialist has called for the U.S. to "immediately dismantle the military industrial complex, cease all imperialist foreign policy, and end all U.S.-led efforts for regime-change," according to his campaign website. Rabb has also called for a universal basic income for Americans as well as guaranteed housing, high-speed internet, free transit and "national grocery stores." He previously took aim at establishment Democrats in an interview with CBS' "Face the Nation" in August, saying, "I think listening to folks who have been institutionalists and corporate Dems is probably the wrong thing to do when what your own poll shows is that there is an exhaustion." Brad Lander, New York Former New York City comptroller Brad Lander is no longer a DSA member, having left the organization over its response to the Oct. 7 attack on Israel by Hamas. But his campaign was backed by some of the DSA's biggest stars, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Lander's campaign for New York's 10th congressional district, which includes downtown Manhattan and parts of Brooklyn, served as a proxy battle between the Empire State's establishment left and socialist factions. While Lander was backed by Mamdani, his primary opponent, Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., was backed by Jeffries. Lander also campaigned alongside Chevalier and Valdez. While he left the DSA over Israel, Lander has still been a fierce critic of the Jewish state. He was recently detained by Israeli law enforcement during a trip to the occupied West Bank to join Palestinian olive farmers harvesting their crop. Israeli authorities released him upon learning his identity. articles.title: Photos: Celebration and gloom as blue wave sweeps midterms
articles.summary: Joy and despair punctuated election watch parties overnight after a blue tsunami swept the country’s midterm elections.
articles.body: Joy and despair punctuated election watch parties overnight after a blue tsunami swept the country’s midterm elections. In Detroit, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed celebrated his victory over Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim senator in U.S. history. He was cheered on by a crowd of supporters — some wearing hijabs, others cowboy hats. There were contrasting scenes of disappointment at a Detroit watch party for Rogers who lost in the hostile race. In Austin, Texas, James Talarico supporters greeted the beaming Democrat at a burger joint after he flipped a Senate seat that had been held by Republicans for decades. Not all Republican gatherings were forlorn. Trump ally Byron Donalds defeated Democrat David Jolly to become Florida’s next governor. In Georgia, Democrat Jon Ossoff cruised to Senate re-election as he defeated Republican Mike Collins. Democrat Roy Cooper bested former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley to win the Senate election in North Carolina, gaining a crucial seat for his party in the race to control the chamber. Democrat Jocelyn Benson succeeded Gretchen Whitmer to become the next governor of Michigan, extending the party’s control for four more years.

articles.title: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker rolls out a Day One road map for Congress
articles.summary: Putting down a marker ahead of a potential presidential bid, Pritzker says the new Democratic Congress must swiftly advance an aggressive legislative agenda.
articles.body: With Democrats set to take control of Congress with a resounding mandate for change, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is urging his party to act swiftly — with Trump-like speed — to advance an aggressive legislative and oversight agenda. To help them along, he is out with a road map for what Congress should tackle the moment they’re sworn in. Fresh off a victory for a third gubernatorial term and looking toward a potential run for president in 2028, Pritzker is set to release a detailed 75-page plan Wednesday, with ideas on everything from increasing the federal minimum wage to restoring SNAP and Medicaid cuts. The plan, which the governor has spent months crafting, was first shared with NBC News. “I believe that on Day One — and I literally mean Day One — that they should begin to introduce legislation. ... I’m looking for very quick action,” Pritzker said in an interview. “I believe that there are big things and small things that need to be done, and they need to be done swiftly.” Follow live updates on the midterm elections Pritzker’s release of a comprehensive policy initiative the day after the midterm elections sets in motion what will be intense jockeying among potential 2028 contenders to stand out in what is expected to be a crowded field. And it sets down a marker for Pritzker, digging into policy at a pivotal moment as the party is looking toward next steps. Pritzker, 61, spent millions on battleground races in the midterms. Recently, he gave $1 million to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in her bid to oust Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. It was a move that won Pritzker goodwill with Hispanic political leaders. With two months before the new Congress convenes, Pritzker has 200 items he believes Democrats should tackle immediately. He pointed to the urgency of Trump’s first days in office in 2025, when the president issued a slew of executive orders and imposed wide-reaching agency policies. Now that voters have spoken, Pritzker said, Democrats need to demonstrate they heard the call for change and are capable of taking actions that don’t drag into interminable battles. “Even if Trump vetoes a restoration of those programs, they should pass it,” he said. “It needs to be clear that this is the direction that the country wants to go, and if Donald Trump wants to stand in the way, that’s obviously on him. But we’ve got to pass these.” Though the road map Pritzker assembled is called “Fighting for Illinois: The Day One Agenda,” it has federal policy and funding recommendations that could pertain to all states. He told NBC News that some weighty issues like comprehensive immigration reform are not on the list because they are complex issues that would involve longer-term discussions. But Pritzker’s plan does call for ending “indiscriminate and outsized immigration round-ups and the mass deportation agenda, strengthen oversight, pursue accountability, and advance common sense immigration reform.” Pritzker also pushes for a boost to the federal minimum wage, which now stands at $7.25 an hour, as a contender for one of Democrats’ first acts. How high it should be raised is something that lawmakers should hash out, he said. In Illinois, the minimum wage is $15 an hour and Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton — who served as his lieutenant governor and received his heavy backing in the Senate race — has called for a $25-an-hour minimum wage. “It should be proposed right away, and there should be hearings and committee votes on that nearly right away. It’s been too long,” Pritzker said. “It’s something we can get done in relatively short order because I believe every Democrat agrees that the minimum wage is too low.” Also on Pritzker’s list is passing the Tariff Relief for Consumer Act, which would require large corporations that received refunds to show how they’re passing them on to consumers. The governor began preparing the agenda in the summer, when he directed state agencies and deputy governors to go through the Trump administration’s cuts to federal programs and grants under Trump that had the greatest impact on Illinois residents and to specify how the 120th Congress could reverse the damage. Among the other recommendations from Pritzker: giving states more authority on betting markets, restoring Temporary Protected Status for immigrants and year-round production on E15 gasoline (a blend of 15% ethanol and 85% gasoline). Pritzker said it would raise ethanol demand, helping Illinois’ agricultural sector while lowering prices at the pump. Asked how Democrats, if they take power, should balance holding administration officials accountable versus attempting to advance new initiatives, Pritzker said that the committees could take the lead on any investigations. “There are committees that can do the exposure of the corruption, the oversight of the executive branch. Those are specific committees in the House of Representatives and in the Senate, and I think they should do their work,” Pritzker said. “But there is work to be done for the working families of America to reverse the damage that Donald Trump has done to them. And I think this Congress has got to get to work on that right away.”
